WITNESS IX
Sr. ANNA CELSA SPERANZA

Scope in the process: From Sess. 146[...] of 5 June 1915 (fol. 1285) to Sess. 156 of 25 June 1915 (fol. 1371); from Sess. 251[...] of 11 December 1916 (fol. 2133v.) to Sess. 258[...] of 3 January 1917 (fol. 2190); Sess. 260[...] of 15 January 1917 (fol. 2208); Sess. 262[...] of 18 January 1917 (fol. 2225); Sess. 265[...] of 25 January 1917 (f. 2251); Sess. 267[...] of 31 January 1917 (f. 2269v.); Sess. 270[...] of 3 February 1917 (f. 2294v.) to Sess. 272[...] of 13 February 1917 (f. 2310); Sess. 278[...] of 1 March 1917 (f. 2372); from Sess. 280[...] of 3 March 1917 (fol. 2389v.) to Sess. 282[...] of 8 March 1917 (f. 2405v.); Sess. 285[...] of 22 March 1917 (f. 2432); from Sess. 288[...] of 30 March 1917 (f. 2455v.) to Sess. 294[...] of 23 April 1917 (f. 2487v.).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Carolina Speranza, born on 30 June 1853 at Sassuolo Modenese.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

State and profession: Religious of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Secretary General. Elected Superior General on 21 October 1915. Age of the witness when she met the Servant of God: 23 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness met her: 45 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 62/64 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness met the Servant of God on 4 November 1876, when she entered the institute of the Daughters of St. Anne at Piacenza; from then on she was very close to the Mother Foundress, especially from 1883, when she called her to her side in the secretariat of the Generalate House.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The long acquaintance and the filial affection that bound the witness for many years to her Superior General result in another particularly extensive testimony, so much so as to lead us to make indispensable cuts.

The first precise information concerns the birth, the family and the youthful years of Gattorno, up to the marriage imposed on her by her parents; this second period too — the marital one — is treated with abundant detail. Passing to the time of widowhood, we find previously unknown information on the socio-apostolic activity intensely carried out in Genoa, followed immediately by the pressing call to give life to a religious foundation, for the determination of which the urgings of the Holy Father Pius IX and of the Archbishop of Genoa were essential. The history of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne is treated very carefully, and from the facts the wisdom and prudence of the Servant of God emerge clearly.

The most extensive subject and the richest in detail proves once again to be the virtuous exercise, where for each virtue a long series of concrete information is reported, the fruit of direct knowledge. The treatment of the supernatural gifts, of the last illness, of the death and of the reputation for holiness is very extensive.

The witness reports many cases of miraculous healings attributed to the intercession of the Servant of God: of these healings only one is reported here.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1289v., testis respondit:

§ 382
Particulars of the witness.

My name in religion is Anna Celsa Speranza, in the world Carolina, of the late Costanzo and Bettina Colombini. I was born at Sassuolo Modenese on 30 June of the year 1853. I was brought up religiously in the family. At twelve I made my first Communion, and then there was born in my heart the liveliest desire to enter Religion. I entered Religion among the Daughters of St. Anne on 4 November 1876. I made my Novitiate at Piacenza for only about fifteen days, and the rest I made here in Rome, at the Parrocchietta outside Porta Portese, and in 1878 I made simple vows at Piacenza. To the Parrocchietta I was sent as Superior and Teacher, having the diploma. I remained there until 1882; however, when the Servant of God was in Rome, she called me to her side to help the Secretary.

§ 383
Scope of knowledge.

Ad 7: From my Confessor, Canon Parish Priest D. Agostino Ferri, still living, and from Fr. Alessandro da Piacenza, Capuchin, now deceased, I first heard of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne; and by the Capuchin Father I was invited to enter her Institute, and by my Confessor encouraged.

Having overcome the natural difficulties of my family, I was received at Piacenza by the Servant of God herself, and so I met her personally.

The first impression I had on seeing her was of finding myself before a great and singular soul, and I immediately had the assurance of entrusting myself to one who was more than a mother. This conviction grew in me more and more through the greater knowledge I had by subsequent contact and through my offices which I had from her. Many things, therefore, I shall say from my personal knowledge de visu; not many, however, because the Servant of God was very secretive and most reserved, and especially with me, because, she told me (rightly or wrongly), I had the faculty of intuiting things; other things I shall say because I heard them from persons worthy of belief, such as the late Sr. Anna Carrega, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, the present Mother Vicar, and Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia, and others.

§ 384
Family of the Servant of God.

Ad 9, Proc. fol. 1296: The Servant of God was born in Genoa, I think in the Parish of the Vigne, on 14 October 1831, of Francesco and Adelaide Campanella; I do not know which of the two had had another consort. As far as I know, the parents of the Servant of God were big merchants, and I believe also bankers. The mother was a holy woman; the father, I believe, was rather indifferent in matters of religion, but was very honest and upright, austere in the government of the family. I think I read in some memoir that he, at his death, left part of his estate to pious works.

The Servant of God had a half-sister and two sisters, Giusta and Elisa, still living. The half-sister, by the name of Luigia, I do not know whether she has died. Elisa is very pious, not so the other. She had three brothers, Emanuele, Federico and Francesco. The first was somewhat indifferent in matters of religion and died very young. Federico, a republican, a Garibaldian, would not hear of religion, and died two years ago: he was, however, of excellent heart and honest. The third too is not tender toward religion, but takes his family to Mass. As to Federico, I must note that he was induced by the Servant of God to unite himself religiously with the woman with whom he was living; and I myself was present at the ceremony, celebrated in our house in Vicolo del Piombo here in Rome.

p. 230

Mrs. Adelaide concerned herself especially with the education of her little daughters, whom she raised religiously. The boys soon withdrew from her care.

§ 385
Early years and education of the Servant of God.

Ad 10: I have heard it said, I do not know by whom, that the Servant of God from childhood showed a very lively disposition, but was always at the same time very good and pious. Grown a little older, she busied herself with household chores, I think in particular with the pantry and the wardrobe. I never heard it said that she liked childish games, or that she loved to dress too elegantly; on the contrary, I have heard it said that she dressed only according to her condition and as befitted her family.

I have heard it said that from girlhood she was much given to piety and inclined to beneficence. Since she kept the pantry at home, she took advantage of it to benefit the poor little daughters of the peasants, as I heard from her herself.

At about eleven she approached first Communion; I do not know the particulars.

As to studies, she did those few that were then customary in reasonably well-off families. She had a particular fondness for music, had a most beautiful voice and sang very well, as I have heard from several, and especially from the brother of the Servant of God, Francesco.

§ 386
Diligent and attentive wife and mother.

Ad 11: The Servant of God felt no inclination for marriage: indeed..., and she was induced to it only by the will of the family, as I learned from her herself and from some sister in whom she confided.

It was not she herself who chose the husband, but he was chosen for her by her relatives in the person of Girolamo Custo, her cousin, a rich merchant, good and religious.

Ad 12: It seems to me (vaguely) that the marriage was celebrated at home and that a certain D. Accinelli, recently deceased, assisted at it. I do not know the particulars.

Ad 13: The Servant of God loved her Husband very much and was always submissive to him. She had three children: Carlotta, Alessandro and Francesco, and these last two have died.

p. 231

Carlotta, as the Servant of God told me too, became deaf-mute as a result of convulsions, and her mother attributed it to a punishment from the Lord for having yielded to her relatives, who wanted her married, whereas she should have become a Capuchin nun. This detail I know from Sr. Anna Sorrentino.

The Servant of God placed Carlotta in an Institute for Deaf-mutes in Milan, and I do not know how many years she stayed there.

Alessandro was placed for his education, I think, in Genoa, I do not remember in which Institute. The Servant of God took pains that they be brought up as Christians. The third died as a little child.

§ 387
Death of her husband and of her last son.

Ad 14: After about eight years of marriage Girolamo died. I heard from the Servant of God herself that she nursed him continually in his last illness, which lasted, I think, three months, without ever even undressing. With great resignation she bore the loss. The death of her husband was very Christian, he died resigned. The Servant of God herself told me that when her husband fell ill for the last time, he went to bed with a slight indisposition that gave nothing to fear; but that she, looking at the Jesus of Nazareth they had at the head of the bed, saw it turn into a skeleton. She understood then that her husband would die of that illness, and she suffered greatly, it being the first time she had seen such transformations.

The Servant of God told us Sisters that she suffered very, very much at the death of her husband, although, on the other hand, she should have felt relieved, having regained the freedom to give herself more completely to God, as she had longed to do before marriage.

Ad 15: «While, however, — said the Servant of God, with a sense of humility — I resigned myself easily to the loss of my husband, though with sorrow, I could find no way to resign myself to the loss of my last little child, which occurred very shortly after that of my husband. And my grief was so strong that, to comfort me, my Confessor, D. Firpo, thought it necessary to come often to comfort me at my house every day. I seemed to go mad with grief; I no longer combed my hair, and almost neglected the other two little ones».

I too knew D. Firpo, who was much esteemed and reputed a holy man.

p. 232

§ 388
After her husband's death she devoted herself to piety and the practice of charity.

Ad 16: Having become a widow, the Servant of God withdrew to her home, with her parents. She gave herself to a more retired and pious life and to works of charity, visiting the Hospitals, and especially that of Pammatone, and the sick in their homes. She also concerned herself with the Daughters of Mary, and I do not know well whether it was she who constituted the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary, or an assistant of Frassinetti. The Archbishop of Genoa, Mgr. Charvaz, having come to know the Servant of God as a Lady who had given herself wholly to good works, himself gave her the charge of concerning herself with the Daughters of Mary.

When I went as Superior to the Parrocchietta, the Servant of God, urging me to found a Congregation of the Daughters of Mary, reminded me that she, in Genoa and the surrounding area, had instituted so many groups of Daughters of Mary, giving them a President, and that these Presidents were then convened by her once a month, and she gave them instructions, gave them notices and explanations, etc.

The Servant of God told me that Frassinetti made a manual for the use of the Daughters of Mary and took it to the Archbishop, that he might deign to approve it; but he, not finding it in everything to his full satisfaction, refused. Then Frassinetti, knowing that the Servant of God, Directress of the Daughters of Mary, was so well received by the Archbishop, thought it good to try, through her, to obtain from the Prelate the approval which he had refused to him personally.

The Archbishop, at the entreaties of the Servant of God, at first refused; but then at last he said to her: «Well, if you can find the points for which I do not think I can give approval to this manual, and if you adjust them to my way, I will approve it». The Servant of God understood the arduousness of the undertaking and at first refused even to look for the points not pleasing to the Archbishop, but he imposed it on her.

Agitated, the Servant of God withdrew home and, placing herself before the miraculous Crucifix, which we keep in her room at Piacenza, prayed before it all night, that it might enlighten her. The next morning she brought the manuscript back to the Archbishop, indicating to him the points that he did not like and the adjustments that, in her view, should be made. Then the Archbishop approved.

Proc. fol. 1305v.: In the old archive, in a dark room, thrown in as best as possible, in our house at Piacenza, we found several letters from Genoese Ladies to the Servant of God, from which it appeared that she herself, when she was in the world, had concerned herself also with other Religious Associations, such as those for endangered girls, for the perpetual Adoration of the Most Blessed Sacrament and, I believe, also for Christian Mothers, etc.

Ad 17: That night, in which the Servant of God, as I said yesterday, prayed before her Crucifix that it might give her light for Frassinetti's manual, she told me that she felt an interior movement by which she understood that she should found an Institute.

And it seems to me that she added further that the inspiration of the Lord was so vehement that it obliged her to throw down on paper at once some notes for such a foundation. These notes, however, she wrote as if beside herself, and when she had come completely to herself and read her notes with a cool head, she was assailed by the thought of her children and had such torment that, no longer able to bear the sight of that writing, she put it in a cupboard without looking at it again for some time. The voice of God, however, interiorly gave her no peace, and she then resolved to speak of it to her Confessor D. Firpo; and it seems to me that D. Firpo reproved her for not having told him at once, and advised her to go to the Archbishop to speak to him about it. If I remember well, she did not have the courage to go personally to the Archbishop and preferred to write to him. The Archbishop then sent for her and when he had heard from the Servant of God the particulars of what she had hinted to him in the letter, he told her categorically that this was the will of God and that she should set to work. He added that he would give her notes on the Institute to be founded to a distinguished Prelate to examine it and at once form an internal regulation. These things I learned from the Servant of God herself.

The Servant of God was always atrociously tormented by the thought of her little sons and her old parents. The Archbishop sent Magnasco, then a Canon and afterward his successor in the government of his Diocese, to the Servant of God to come to an understanding with her and form the regulation together. This, however, did not turn out to the full satisfaction of the Servant of God, because, she told me, it did not seem to her in everything in conformity with the inspirations received. For this she took, I do not remember well what pretext, to scuttle everything and declared to the Archbishop that only at the imposition of the Holy Father would she yield. Then the Archbishop obliged her to come to Rome.

§ 390
Journey to Rome and the Pope's attitude toward the new Institute.

Ad 18: The Servant of God yielded to the injunction made to her by the Archbishop. And so as to let nothing be glimpsed by her family she spoke to them of it as of a wish of hers to come and see Rome together with a friend of hers — one of those who with her busied themselves with good works —; and I do not know well whether it was Mrs. Teresa Marazzo or Maddalena Durazzo. The family assented; indeed her father procured her suitable recommendations for making the sea voyage as far as Civitavecchia. The voyage was most stormy to the end. Having put in at Livorno, the Servant of God went ashore to make her Communion, and it was noon; and she made it again the next day at Civitavecchia.

Arrived in Rome, she took lodging with I no longer remember which private family, to which she had been directed before leaving Genoa. To obtain the audience of the Holy Father she had a letter of recommendation from her Archbishop. I do not know whether this letter was addressed to the Holy Father himself. After a few days she had the Pontifical audience. In the private audience, having set before the Holy Father her inspirations and the project so dreaded by her, Pius IX said to her: «It pleases me; these are commandments of God and inspirations of the Lord; set to work and make the regulation on the outline or notes that you felt inspired to write».

The Servant of God, hearing that the Pope spoke in unison with her Archbishop, was at once tormented anew by the thought of her children, and begged the Holy Father to be so good as to dispense her on account of her duties as a Mother. The Pope, however: «No — he added, in a severe tone — I do not dispense you; if you do not heed the voice of God, you will have remorse for all your life». He added further: «Your Institute will extend to the whole world with the flight of a dove, and will last until the end of the ages. God will take care of your little ones».

She then bowed her head at the feet of the Pope, submitted to the heavy yoke that was laid on her, and the Pope, for her comfort, made her a gift of two photographs of himself, which are still preserved at Piacenza.

I do not know whether it was in this first audience or in another, but certainly on the occasion of this first journey to Rome, she asked the Holy Father for some privileges for the Institute she would found, and Pius IX deigned to affix at once his rescript himself, and this rescript is kept in the Archive of this house. I recall that the Servant of God, telling us of it, said to us: «It is very curious that the Institute, before being born, has received privileges».

Despite so much kindness of the Holy Father, so much condescension of his, the Servant of God felt so troubled by the thought of her children that for twenty-four hours she was as if beside herself, and had even lost the sense of touch, and kept repeating: «Ah! my children, my children!».

In so many struggles that the Servant of God had and of which I myself was a witness, I never saw her weep, but when she told us this episode of her life, her eyes grew moist, and she added to us: «But here I am: the Lord wanted me, and here is the beast of burden for the work», or similar expressions.

§ 391
The Ven. Francesco da Camporosso and the foundation.

Proc. fol. 1313: The Servant of God, during her widowhood, and I do not know whether also before, often dealt with the holy Capuchin Lay Brother Francesco da Camporosso, now Venerable, and one day (all this I know from the Servant of God), as if beside herself, after she (perhaps she had questioned him about the future foundation) heard him exclaim: «Oh! poor creature! poor creature! How much you will have to suffer! Oh! how many nuns I see! oh! how many, how many!».

§ 392
Reason why the foundation was made at Piacenza.

Ad 19: The Servant of God, as I know from her herself (and I leave some point undetermined, because she did not tell it to me, and I do not know it otherwise), met a certain D. Luigi Cogrossi, domiciled in Rome (I do not remember well what he did), who, having to make the journey toward Piacenza, induced her to take that road too, instead of returning to Genoa by sea, on which she had suffered so much on the journey coming to Rome. One sees that the Servant of God (having come to know Cogrossi as a good Priest) disclosed to him her project of foundation; and Cogrossi, once arrived at Piacenza, made her acquainted with two good Canons Chiappini. These encouraged her to begin her work in Piacenza rather than in Genoa, and also offered her a house for rent for the beginnings of the work. She hesitated at first, but the project of founding at Piacenza rather than at Genoa smiled on her, although she foresaw the difficulties the Archbishop of Genoa would raise, as well as the family. She returned to Genoa before beginning the work and said nothing of her project in the family. She reported to the Archbishop what had happened and her project of beginning her foundation at Piacenza. And in this regard the Archbishop opposed, in view of the good she was doing in Genoa. The Servant of God insisted, prayed much to her Crucifix, returned to the charge, and then the Archbishop at last acceded.

§ 393
Move to Piacenza and family conflicts.

The Servant of God, having obtained the Archbishop's consent, secretly, with the help of some person, sent much of her belongings and furniture to Piacenza, to the house which, as I said, the Canons Chiappini had offered her. She was able to do it secretly, so she said, because in her father's house a little apartment had been assigned to her on the same floor, separate, and I have seen that little apartment.

This done, she set before the family her plan, and naturally all hell broke loose. Her good mother was especially upset, because, advanced in age and sickly, she saw herself assisted by her daughter with so much love and sacrifice, even at the cost of entire nights of rest. The Servant of God nevertheless showed herself always calm and undaunted. The Servant of God had already gathered for her foundation some Genoese young women, and when the moment of departure came, her good mother, to dissuade her from abandoning her, laid herself stretched out on the threshold of the door (in the memoirs of the Servant of God I found written that her mother sat down on the threshold), saying: «Let us see if you will have the courage to pass over my body». The Servant of God then (it is always she who told me these things) took a leap and flew to the station, where she found the young women summoned by her for her foundation, and with them left for Piacenza. It seems to me that the Servant of God also told us that her Confessor D. Firpo too was at first opposed to her foundation in Piacenza, but then acquiesced.

Ad 20: Of those young women brought with her by the Servant of God to Piacenza, some did not persevere and returned to their homeland.

§ 394
Beginning of the foundation: first companions and title.

Arrived at Piacenza, she at once came to an agreement with the Bishop Mgr. Ranza, who had shown himself very favorable to her on her first visit to that city and had promised her his support.

The little apartment offered her by the Canons Chiappini in Piacenza did not please the Servant of God, and she set out to look for another, more suitable premises. She was then offered the Palazzo Del Verme, which was divided into so many small apartments (so much was afterward spent to adapt it); it is the house where we are even at present, and there she began her foundation.

Of the young women whom the Servant of God had gathered around her, she chose five for the first clothing, which took place on the eighth of December 1866, the Vicar General being present, since the Bishop kept himself absent, as I think I learned from Sr. Anna Redenta. And they are: Sr. Anna Rosa Podestà, Sr. Anna Giovanna Bixio, Sr. Anna Angela Degrossi, Luigia Camisa and a certain Marano. All are dead, and I knew three of them.

The foundation began under the title of Daughters of the Immaculate. The reasons for this title and for its change to Daughters of St. Anne I do not know well enough to say anything; in general I can say that it was because of a vision. I know with certainty, however, that the Servant of God met opposition over the change of name from the Protector of the Sisters of St. Anne, Cardinal Caterini. Yet one day, the Servant of God being received with her Sisters in audience by the Holy Father Pius IX, he, on seeing her, exclaimed: «Oh! here are the Daughters of St. Anne». With this the discussions ended, the opposition ceased and the title of Daughters of St. Anne remained with us. So I heard from Mr. Tornatore.

As to the habit, I know nothing, except that when I entered, instead of wearing in winter the little shawl that we now wear, we wore a kind of black jacket.

The Servant of God did not put on the religious habit with the first five, but on the feast of St. Anne in 1867.

From the Servant of God I did not learn the reason for this delay, but perhaps it was to be freer in business affairs, because I know that she worked with the Mayor and with the Prefect to obtain approval.

§ 395
First meeting with Fr. Tornatore.

Ad 21: As far as I understood and heard from the Servant of God, before the first clothing the Servant of God asked the Bishop for a Priest to give the exercises. From the Bishop or other authoritative persons of Piacenza she was advised to ask Mr. Tornatore, of the Priests of the Mission, who enjoyed a reputation for holiness, who was at S. Lazzaro. To him the Servant of God went and invited him to give this retreat to her daughters. Mr. Tornatore accepted. He himself said that on first seeing her he was struck, having recognized at once in her an extraordinary woman. And I recall that he said further that he had had a vision in which he had seen a procession of Religious, and in front of them one carried the banner; and he added that when he saw the Servant of God he recognized in her precisely the one with the banner. I certainly do not feel able to give any importance to this; the Servant of God herself, when she alluded to this fact, said: «Nonsense, nonsense!».

§ 396
Fr. Tornatore, author of the first unapproved rule.

Proc. fol. 1322: From the documents and letters found in a cupboard in Piacenza one can gather that Pius IX, having learned that the Servant of God had begun her Institute in Piacenza, through Cardinal Patrizi exhorted her again to form an internal regulation for her Sisters. But the Servant of God, humble and diffident about herself as she was, having on the occasion of the first exercises made the acquaintance of Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, as I have already deposed, asked him to be so good as to draw up this internal regulation himself. He set to work and made this regulation in the form of a dialogue between St. Anne and the Religious, and this was presented to the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars for approval.

From the memoirs found likewise in the famous cupboard at Piacenza it emerges that the Servant of God, from 1871, had asked in an audience of the Holy Father for a Protector in the person of His Eminence Vannicelli, then Archbishop of Ferrara, and that the Holy Father granted it to her. From the same memoirs and letters it is known that Cardinal Vannicelli and his Secretary Wanstienkist worked hard for the approval of the said regulation.

Considerable time passed with the procedures for approval. And when it seemed that the difficulties had been overcome, Cardinal Vannicelli was informed that the regulation had passed to the Holy Office, and that the Holy Office had ordered that all the copies of that regulation be burned and that Fr. Tornatore be removed from our Institute. And from the Servant of God herself I learned the sorrow she felt on receiving such news from the Cardinal Protector. The Servant of God told me (and when she told me something, sometimes other Sisters of the Secretariat were present too), she said to me: «The sorrow I felt on receiving that letter is inexpressible, and to carry out the obedience of withdrawing at once all the copies of the regulation I stayed up all night to send the order to all our houses to send the regulation to me, which I then wished to burn myself».

I believe that the Bishop of Piacenza himself, or else the Cardinal Protector, communicated the order of the Holy Office to Fr. Tornatore, who felt great sorrow, but nevertheless withdrew.

§ 397
Relations of the Servant of God with Fr. Tornatore at the beginning of the foundation.

Now I shall speak of the relations that had existed between Mr. Tornatore and the Servant of God. She found herself without the help of her former Confessor, D. Firpo, who had washed his hands of everything concerning the Servant of God when she thought she must make her foundation at Piacenza (and in fact no correspondence between the Servant of God and D. Firpo has been found after that time); on the other hand, the Servant of God felt the need, in a City new to her, of a support which she believed she had found in that learned and undoubtedly holy man who was Mr. Tornatore; on the other hand again, Mr. Tornatore had for her the greatest esteem and veneration and was ready to do all he could to help her in spirit and also materially, as he showed by the subsidies and alms he procured for her from others. She therefore relied on him for her foundation, chose him as guide and Director and sometimes also confessed to him. In her humility the Servant of God took counsel with him in the most important matters, but the government of her Institute she reserved to herself. In the early times she also made some journey with Mr. Tornatore, and some winter, as the Servant of God spent it in Rome, she had Mr. Tornatore come to Rome as well.

At first Fr. Tornatore at Piacenza came to our house in the morning and went away in the evening, and for some time he also stayed overnight in our house, but with the Bishop's permission. In honor of the truth I must say that Mr. Tornatore, on those nights when he was in our house, spent them almost entirely in the Chapel before the Most Blessed Sacrament, and I myself noticed it on those occasions when I was with the Mother.

In Rome, however, when he came, he went to his Confreres, with whom, however, not feeling at ease, the Servant of God allowed herself to be induced to assign him a room in our house, and he always followed his system of spending almost the whole night in the Chapel. Of when he stayed overnight in our house at Piacenza I can relate what the Servant of God herself told us, laughing. At a certain hour of the night the Servant of God went to pray in the Chapel, but in the little gallery above, and from there she surprised good Tornatore who, turned toward St. Anne, made gestures of filial threat to her and spoke with her. Sometimes she saw Mr. Tornatore light all the candles of the Altar (and the Servant of God was seized by fear of fire, because Mr. Tornatore was very short-sighted) and, this done, he began his animated talking with St. Anne.

§ 398
Fr. Tornatore's mystical exaltation.

This already shows the mystical exaltation of this good religious, and how rightly the Servant of God smiled in telling it to us.

I have heard it said, further, that Mr. Tornatore took advantage a little too much of the Servant of God's inclination to penances and fasts to push her further, and that at times he addressed hard and harsh reproaches to her. For this the Servant of God was advised not to use him as Director, and she followed the advice.

The Servant of God was informed of the order of the Holy Office concerning the regulation while she was in Piacenza. She therefore thought it opportune to come to Rome to know how she should proceed and had audience also with the Holy Father (in her dealings she was always helped by the Cardinal Protector, to whom we owe so much).

§ 399
Advised by Pius IX, the Servant of God prepares a new rule.

Pius IX received her, as she herself told, with such affability. «I find you worn out — he said to her — but you must not lose heart. You yourself will redo the regulation, but hold firm to the spirit of the first».

The Servant of God left the audience much consoled and comforted, and the regulation was drawn up by her under the guidance of the Cardinal Protector, at Ferrara, as I know from the Mother herself. However, the immediate help for the drafting of the regulation she had from Mgr. Giordano, who afterward succeeded Vannicelli in the Archbishopric of Ferrara. Vannicelli himself had assigned him to her as immediate help. This I know from the written memoirs and from the Servant of God herself.

§ 400
Sufferings of the Servant of God until the approval of the constitutions.

The Servant of God then dwelt in our house which we already had at Ferrara from that time, but either from the moral sufferings caused by the communication of the order of the Holy Office, or from the damp air of that City, or from all together, she fell ill and her whole head swelled, suffering atrocious pains. She nevertheless worked all the same, the Servant of God, and completed the regulation, which was then sent at once to Rome, and she returned to Piacenza. Some difficulties arose over certain points of the regulation in the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, but they were overcome, and the decree of praise of the Institute came out. The Servant of God then desired to have the decree of approval of the Institute and had it, but the Congregation for the approval of Rules set as a condition that some animadversions and additions be accepted. The Servant of God convened in 1881 at Piacenza all the Superiors (we were 74) to make us accept what the Holy Congregation desired. The Capitulars, however, on hearing those animadversions and additions, swallowed them badly. Mgr. Scalabrini presided over the Chapter, who perhaps was not very practiced in such matters, and when Cardinal Ferrieri, Prefect of Bishops and Regulars, learned that the Sisters did not so willingly accept the said animadversions and additions, he made great threats, even of taking from us the privileges and the decrees of praise and approval of the Institute, but all was settled with the help of Cardinal Alimonda, then our Protector, and of Mgr. Laurenzi, Auditor of His Holiness. Instead of convening the Capitulars again, ballot papers were sent to them, both for the election of the Assistants and the Secretary General and for the other matters concerning the Institute. Two Sessions were then held in the house of Cardinal Alimonda himself, and finally the rules were reprinted with various additions in accordance with the wishes of the Holy Congregation, though not all. With this the Servant of God believed that approval would not be refused, but the Congregation wanted them all.

Proc. fol. 1331: In the preceding session I said that concerning the Constitutions or regulation drawn up by the Servant of God at Ferrara, difficulties arose in the Holy Congregation over certain points. On reflection, I find I must correct it thus: the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars wished to modify the constitutions, and advised the Servant of God to keep in a new drafting to those of the Stigmatine Sisters and of the Dorotheans, and said that Fr. Fava, a Jesuit, would be suitable to elaborate the said constitutions. The Servant of God bowed her head, but together begged the Holy Congregation to be so good as to grant her that Fr. Fava, before making those constitutions, go to Piacenza to study the Institute and its spirit. She was answered that the said Father was old, in poor health, very busy. The Servant of God replied, begging that they would add two other Consultors, asking together that before setting to work they should have heard her. Of this new proposal too nothing was done. Time passed, and she felt distressed because meanwhile her Sisters had no rule at all; therefore she wrote to Mgr. Vitelleschi, declaring to him first of all that she was ready to bow her head to what the Church wanted, but that together she felt strongly distressed and tempted to lay everything down. Following this, the conclusion was reached: the Holy Congregation ordered that she withdraw her constitutions as they had been drawn up by her, and that her Institute follow them ad experimentum. The Constitutions were to be printed with the nihil obstat of the Cardinal Protector Vannicelli. Then came out the decree of praise of the Institute, etc., with all the rest, as I said in the preceding session.

I must add further that in 1885 the constitutions were reprinted with all the additions and modifications wanted by the Holy Congregation, which gave them ad experimentum for ten years.

What has been said so far I gathered partly from documents and partly from the Servant of God herself.

§ 401
The constitutions are approved in 1892: joy in the Institute.

In 1891 Alimonda died and was succeeded in our Protectorship by Cardinal Verga, Prefect of the Holy Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. The Servant of God, whose desire was to leave the Institute definitively settled with the Constitutions before dying, and in order not to leave to others an inheritance of anxieties and sorrows, which she had already experienced, went at once to the new Cardinal Protector, begging him to be so good as to obtain for her at once the definitive approval of the rules with those modifications that she saw as necessary. The modifications and additions that had been previously imposed by the Holy Congregation had not given a good result. The Cardinal showed her that it was very difficult to obtain what she desired. But without saying anything to the Servant of God he set to work. I, then, reflecting that the following year (1892) would be the twenty-fifth anniversary of the foundation of our Institute, took the liberty, speaking with the Cardinal Protector, of saying to him: «Oh! what a fine gift it would be for our Mother if Your Eminence, next year, the twenty-fifth of our foundation, could obtain for her the definitive approval of our rules!». «Nonsense, nonsense», answered the Cardinal, but nevertheless he worked. From time to time he stopped with the Servant of God to speak of the rules. Thus he came to know one by one the modifications she desired and the relevant reasons. Once a Consultor of his Holy Congregation came to the Servant of God (sent, it is understood, by the Cardinal) to speak to her and question her on the constitutions; but she did not understand why, although she suspected something. The Cardinal had worked so briskly and effectively that the Constitutions by the feast of St. Anne in 1892 were definitively approved, according to the wishes of the Servant of God.

On 26 July His Eminence Verga came to say Mass in the private Chapel of our Institute, which was then on the second floor; and before Mass, having called the Secretary Sr. Benedetta Carrega and me, handing us the rules, he said to us: «Here are the approved rules, and I hope the Mother will be pleased with them. After Mass, in the Corridor, bring the rules to me in the presence of the Mother, for I wish to present them to her».

Sr. Benedetta Carrega then gave the order to the Sisters (we were very many, because so many had come from elsewhere for that day) to line up in the Corridor for the Cardinal's passage. After Mass, as he came out of the Chapel, Sr. Benedetta and I held out to him on a tray the rules, which he took and, handing them to the Mother, said to her: «Your wishes are now fulfilled. Here are the rules definitively approved». The Servant of God was beside herself with joy; she pressed the rules to her breast and, unable to contain the rush of her feelings, fled to hide on the first floor. She lost on that occasion her Crucifix and the bows. We all, meanwhile, burst into tears; Sr. Benedetta, who never left her, tried to reach the Mother, but could not find her, and this made her despair. His Eminence too was moved and went down afterward to the Secretariat. When the Servant of God had regained her calm, she presented herself to His Eminence to thank him, declaring herself unworthy of so great a favor. And the Cardinal: «It is not you who must give thanks — he said — but it is the Church that must thank you, because the Institute is no longer yours, but belongs to the Church».

§ 402
The Servant of God, superior general until her death.

Ad 22: The Superior General of the Institute was always the Servant of God, Mother Gattorno. Before the Chapter held in the year 1888 under the Presidency of Cardinal Alimonda I heard it said by Sr. Benedetta Carrega that the Servant of God had been confirmed by the Holy Father Leo XIII as Superior General for life. Carrega was present at an audience of Pope Leo XIII, in which the Pope himself told the Servant of God that she must be Superior General for life. The facts corresponded to this will of the Pope, for neither in the Chapter of 1888 nor in the following Chapters was there ever any talk of the election or confirmation of the Mother General, while the other offices were discussed. The Servant of God, however, did not feel vainly flattered by such an office; she shrank from hearing herself called General and, if it was at times necessary to add it to her signature for the authority of the acts, she signed simply Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno, and the title of General the Secretary was obliged to add. She also showed displeasure when she read the title of General in the address of her daughters.

§ 403
She carried out her duties with diligence, zeal and charity.

The Servant of God carried out her office with diligence, with zeal, with love, with charity, and, when the occasion at times required it, also with rigor. In receiving Postulants into the Institute she gave great consideration to whether they came from good families and had lived with their mother. She preferred these to those educated in Institutes, even by Religious. She took no account of riches and nobility.

From some person who persecuted the Institute I heard it said that the Servant of God was too easy in admitting Postulants in the early times; to me, however, this easiness is not at all evident. The Servant of God had a penetrating and sure intuition and a just judgment, so that very rarely did it happen that she was mistaken in accepting those who presented themselves to her. It happened to her, indeed, more often to suffer some disappointment over those who had been accepted by other local Superiors, to whom she had given her consent.

§ 404
The Servant of God was accused of too much ease in accepting postulants.

Proc. fol. 1340: As to the alleged ease in accepting Postulants in the beginnings of the Institute, besides what I have said, I add further that the Servant of God, speaking to me precisely of the beginnings, told me that as soon as the news of the new foundation spread, a very great number of young women applied to enter it. I do not know afterward whether all who applied were accepted. The fact is that almost all of those admitted remained in the Institute and that their religious spirit was the life and soul of our Institute.

§ 405
On the contrary, she acted with great prudence in the whole of her government.

His Eminence Serafini himself said to various persons (and among these, if I remember well, to Mgr. Piscicelli, Abbot of S. Nicola at Bari), on the occasion of the Apostolic visitation he made: «The Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, as long as the old element lasts, will go well».

In receiving Postulants I know that she mostly asked information from Parish Priests. She also wanted all the certificates in order, and as I recall, she asked counsel of the Assistants too.

From the very beginnings of the foundation of the Institute I learned from other Sisters that she visited the Houses very often and was always here and there, so that once, asked what her domicile was, she answered jokingly: «On the railways».

The continuity of her visits can be gathered from the itinerary of the Servant of God, which I, at the request of this Tribunal, compiled last year. For the visit to the houses she did not shrink from discomforts and sacrifices.

The Servant of God was always subjected to the cross and to suffering, and always suffered either morally or physically; but never did sufferings stop her in her visits to the houses of the Institute.

In the visits she took great care to see whether the religious spirit was maintained. Once I recall she had to suffer because she met a Bishop who would have wished to modify some points of the Constitutions; but she fought and won.

With her searching eye she guessed well when in the houses there was something not in conformity with the spirit, tried to apply a prompt remedy, and often had recourse to the means of changing Sisters.

§ 406
In distributing offices she avoided partiality toward persons.

Proc. fol. 1350v.: The Servant of God, in distributing offices to the Sisters, never showed partiality of persons nor secondary ends, but chose according as she judged them more suitable.

I have heard it said, perhaps from Cardinal Verga, that the Servant of God was accused of some partiality toward this or that Sister, but I could not take such accusations into serious consideration and, coming down to the particulars on which I am questioned, I shall speak first of all of Sr. Anna Maria Teresa Sorrentino. She, having entered the Institute in 1892, once the year of Novitiate was over, was admitted by the Servant of God as a helper in the General Secretariat and, in the Chapter of 1895 presided over by Cardinal Verga, although she had not yet made perpetual vows, was elected Assistant General, and the Cardinal himself took care of the dispensation, which was necessary on account of the perpetual vows she had not yet made. First of all she was a cultured Religious, of much talent, and moreover, although she entered when she was over 30, she was nonetheless a very good Religious, observant and very pious. She also much enjoyed the trust of the Servant of God and was for her a sort of Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia. This suffices to justify the Servant of God against anything that may have been said of her partiality. As for me, I know of no influence of the Servant of God at all on the Capitulars in the election of the Assistants General.

§ 407
Charity toward those struck by cholera and among the poor. Poverty at the beginning of the foundation: rapid development of the Institute.

Ad 23, Proc. fol. 1357v.: The Servant of God, as soon as her foundation had begun, had to look after the daughters of those who had been struck by cholera, and many she took into her house; then she began to go herself and to send her Sisters to assist the poor sick in their homes, bringing them linen and anything else they needed. Then, as the Sisters grew in number, she opened another house, which I think was given by the Municipality, and there, with the means given by the benefactors of Piacenza, especially by the Marquis Landi, a nursery school for poor children was set up. In this building, on the top floor, the somewhat sickly Sisters were also placed.

Typhus having then broken out in Piacenza, the Servant of God sent the Sisters to assist the typhus patients, and so that the disease might not be contracted by all the sisters, she sent the nurses of the typhus patients to live in this nursery.

The Servant of God was then invited to send her Sisters to the hospital of Cento, and because of the acute anticlericalism that reigned in that place at that time, she sent them dressed as lay women, and she too went up and down from Piacenza to Cento, with so many sacrifices and frights, as she herself told, because there was a good stretch to be covered in a little gig. It must be noted that the Servant of God was very attractive, and was still dressed as a lay woman at that time.

I have heard it said that another was then opened at Sampierdarena, in the family villa of the Servant of God, and this foundation I also found in the books.

I have heard it said that at Nizza Monferato, where in the beginnings of the Institute our Sisters were sent, the house assigned for their lodging being very cramped, the Servant of God, when she went there for that foundation, chose for her rest a bed from which a corpse had just been removed. I recall that the Servant of God once only barely alluded to the stench she had smelled.

The Institute developed rapidly because the work of the Sisters was very welcome, and especially because they went to assist the sick, without being able to accept even a drop of water. Moreover, the Servant of God went begging herself in Piacenza, and in this City, however, she did not send the Sisters. When the Institute then spread beyond Piacenza, she sent the Sisters there to beg as well.

§ 409
Sufferings from gossip and financial straits.

I have heard it said that the Servant of God suffered in the beginnings of the Institute because she was opposed by gossip such as this: that this new Institute was a commercial speculation of hers.

I have heard it said that likewise in the beginnings she had to suffer from financial straits, and that miraculously, or almost, she was relieved of them. I have heard it said, if I remember well, that once, when there was lacking, I do not know well whether the bread or the pasta, in the house at Piacenza, the cook having presented herself to the Servant of God to tell her what was lacking, the Servant of God was not disturbed, but answered: «The Lord will provide». In fact, shortly afterward, behold a Benefactor sends or brings what is necessary.

The Institute spread rapidly in northern Italy, and then came to Rome, where, in the times precisely of struggle for the constitutions, three popular schools dependent on Pius IX were opened.

§ 410
First house in Rome.

That of the Parrocchietta, outside Porta Portese, in 1872-73; another outside Porta Cavalleggeri at the Madonna del Riposo, in the same years; and the third in Via di Tor de' Specchi, always in those years. Here the Oblates had given a part of the premises. In those same times another house was opened which concerned itself especially with domestic servants, in Via della Lungara. In Vicolo Margana another house was then opened in the year, I think, 1876-77, where the Mother lodged when she came to Rome. From here the Sisters went to assist the sick in their homes, and here a small Boarding School was also opened afterward.

§ 411
Expansion of the Institute abroad.

Until 1878 the Institute developed only in Italy, and in that year the first expedition of Sisters was made to the hospital of La Paz in Bolivia, where they developed rapidly.

In 1886 our Sisters were then sent also to the Italian colony of Eritrea, where the schools were entrusted to us. And in this colony too they developed rapidly. And oh! would that we had enough Sisters to send them both to America and to Africa, whence continual requests come to us!

p. 248

The Servant of God at her death left three hundred houses of her Institute.

Before accepting new houses the Servant of God first asked the consent of the Ordinary; and for the spiritual part of jurisdiction she always wanted her Sisters to turn to the Bishop of the place. When, with the administrations of hospitals or of other pious bodies, the Servant of God, even after the Sisters had entered, did not find herself in agreement and could not adapt to the new demands of the lay administration, or because they did not keep to the original contracts, she did not stay there to discuss much, but withdrew them.

§ 412
Prudence and wisdom at the base of the foundation.

Proc. fol. 1366: As to the relations of the Generalate House with the others, the Servant of God wanted that, in what was of episcopal jurisdiction, they should depend on the Ordinaries, but in what concerned the internal running, they should depend on her.

In the contracts she made with the Administration of pious Bodies or of schools, she always reserved the right to change the personnel when she thought it opportune. The Servant of God kept up a large correspondence with the local Superiors and demanded to be informed often on the running of their houses. If some delayed, she did not fail to shake her up.

As to the financial relations of the Generalate House with the others, the Servant of God prescribed that what exceeded their needs they should remit to the Generalate House, and she wanted the general accounting.

§ 413
Vigilance over religious observance and poverty.

As far as I know, I know, and I heard from the Servant of God herself and from Mr. Tornatore, that she inculcated on the local Superiors the observance of the rules, and above all of poverty; adding that those houses which observed the vow of poverty most were the ones that went best, and that gave more too to the generalate house, without making the Sisters suffer.

I have heard it said, unfortunately, by persons outside the Institute, whom I could not identify, that the Servant of God favored those Superiors who sent more money to the Generalate House and exalted them, even though the Sisters of these Superiors suffered; but these people certainly did not know our affairs, and I, who was for so long at the side of the Servant of God, never noticed anything that could constitute the slightest basis for this charge.

That the Mother favored those Superiors who more observed the spirit of poverty is true; that she favored those who, as a consequence, ran their houses better, is also true; but that directly or indirectly the Servant of God opposed the local Superiors who sent less money and obliged them to send more, even with suffering to their subjects, this is not true.

The fact, however, is that those who better observed the vow of poverty had, as I said, more money to send to the Servant of God, while their houses went better also temporally and without suffering on the part of the subjects (as we still see happening in our houses today), and these Superiors the Servant of God favored, certainly not because they sent more money.

§ 414
Reply to a charge concerning financial aid to the Generalate house.

I have heard it said that this charge was made by the Apostolic Visitor, now Cardinal Serafini. He, when he went to the houses, listened to all the Sisters: no wonder that some discontented ones were found among them, but again I exclude that the Servant of God was governed by that spirit and performed deeds that could give foundation to these charges. Both I and Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, who also stood close to the Servant of God, think in the same way, and the said Sister spoke to me in this sense. As to the late general Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, I cannot recall with certainty whether she spoke to me of this charge, but from the whole of her discourses, and from the very high esteem she had for the Servant of God, to whom she was so attached that she could not be without her for even a moment, I must conclude that on this point she was of my opinion and of that of Sr. Camilla.

If something more precise comes to my mind, I shall say it another time.

§ 415
Complaints about lack of necessities and their explanation.

I remember complaints about lack of necessities on the part of the Sisters reaching our Secretariat during the government of Mother Carrega, who cannot truly be charged with stinginess on this point, and it was necessary to hold firm, because these complaints, had they been heeded, would have given rise to grave abuses; but I do not at present recall that similar complaints reached us during the government of the Servant of God, and this difference comes from the greater disciplinary rigor that reigned under her government. When the Servant of God went visiting the houses, she listened one by one to all the Sisters and also questioned them chiefly on whether they were well treated at table and whether they lacked necessities. This I know, because I heard it said afterward when she went on visitation.

It was enough to see what abundant portions she herself served when she went into the kitchen: she served them so abundant that they were the despair of the cooks, because sometimes it happened that the necessary was lacking at the second table and it had to be remedied as best one could. In the visits to the houses I myself saw sometimes, and in others I heard it said, that the Servant of God also concerned herself with the good treatment of the girls we kept in our Boarding Schools, Orphanages, etc. When the visits were over, the Servant of God gathered the Sisters of the House to give them a conference, in which she touched on the points that the visit itself suggested to her, and in these conferences, when she saw fit, she spoke of the good treatment of the Sisters and of the girls. Of these conferences we have found some notes, in which she alludes «for House A, so-so, for House B, so and so», and we keep them in the room of the Servant of God. After these conferences, the Sisters came out enraptured.

§ 416
Reply of the Servant of God to a momentary discontent in the community.

I have heard it said by elderly Sisters, I no longer remember which, that before I entered the Institute the Servant of God, visiting the houses, found some discontent, I do not know precisely arising from what; then the Servant of God gathered all the local Superiors in our House at Piacenza, and the Bishop himself, Mgr. Scalabrini, gave the exercises. During these exercises the Servant of God treated the Sisters with an altogether extraordinary interest and kindness. When the exercises were over, having these Superiors with her, she said to them: «Now then, we are agreed. As you have been treated here, so you must treat your Sisters».

As to her concern for the sick Sisters, I have found a little page of regulation written by the Servant of God, and from this document, which we still keep, it appears how great was her concern and her charity toward them.

She also took care to visit them personally, to comfort and assist them, and oh how many she cured!

Ad 24, Proc. fol. 1373v.: From what I have heard said, I know that the Servant of God, when she became a Religious, had her son Alessandro in a College at Savona and her deaf-mute daughter in an Institute for Deaf-Mutes at Milan.

It was told me by the elderly Sisters that Alessandro, when he learned that his mother had become a Religious, fell into a fit of madness. He broke windowpanes and other things. The Mother, however, succeeded in calming him and had him make his first Communion, and he was not even disturbed when he afterward saw her dressed as a Sister.

I do not remember well whether the Servant of God sent him back at once to the College or handed him over to his grandfather; it is certain that he did not remain at Piacenza.

When the education of her daughter Carlotta was finished, the Servant of God took her back with her, hoping to induce her to become a Religious, and it seemed that Carlotta inclined toward the Sacramentine Sisters, who then lived beside the Quirinal and are now in Via di S. Lucia in Selci. But nothing came of it, and she declared that she wanted a husband. After this declaration the Servant of God, seeing all her labor in vain, often entrusted her to a family of the Counts Marazzani of Piacenza, a very Christian family, and so she found someone who asked for her in marriage, and this was Count Gaspare Barbiellini-Amidei.

As to Carlotta's dowry, I can say only this particular: when the father of the Servant of God died, the villa that her family had at Sampierdarena fell to her, and this villa was sold at a price double what it was worth before, because the railway administration needed it. What else fell to the Servant of God in inheritance and to Carlotta as dowry, I do not know. Carlotta was already married when I entered the Institute. Rarely did the Servant of God speak of this marriage, and she always spoke of it with anguish, because she would have wished, as I said, that Carlotta become a nun, and she always said that she was her cross. And I believe she was her cross not only because she was deaf-mute, but also because of the inevitable family troubles in those sad conditions, troubles that the daughter always communicated to the Servant of God. I must add further that she was suspicious and irascible.

§ 418
Suffering of the Servant of God over her son Alessandro.

As I have heard it said, her son Alessandro, grown up, wished to go to America; the mother suffered greatly. After a certain time Alessandro returned from America and went into a certain business, of which he soon tired. He then took a large property on lease, during which time his illness of consumption developed, and at thirty-five he died. This leased property was in the Piacenza countryside, and he lived in Piacenza in a little house in Via del Vescovado, and there he died.

The Servant of God, when her son worsened, was in Rome and charged the Superior of the Mother House at Piacenza to assist, and have her Sisters assist, her son. Alessandro, however, wanted his mother, and Mgr. Scalabrini sent a telegram to the Servant of God inviting her to go there. After this telegram the Servant of God set out, and was at her son's bedside. (It is my impression that without that telegram from the Bishop the Servant of God would not have moved, either because she knew him to be in good hands, or because she believed he would not die so soon). The son recovered a little, and then the Servant of God returned to Rome; but not long after she was called back again by the Bishop of Piacenza. Returned to Piacenza, she stayed there until her son's death, who lived still nearly three months; and she went in the morning from the Mother House to her son's house, and returned in the evening.

§ 419
Even though anguished over her son, she never neglected her duty as superior.

In this time of anguish over the condition of her son, the Servant of God did not at all neglect her duties as Mother General of her Institute; she kept the correspondence with her Sisters alive; she sent visitors where there was need, and even arranged an expedition of eight Sisters to New York, to be sent with the Missionaries of Mgr. Scalabrini, who had requested them of her. Of all this I myself am a witness, for I was then with the Mother at Piacenza. Admirable thing! Her son died a day or two before the departure of the Sisters, and so it happened that, while in our Chapel, in the presence of the Servant of God, Mgr. Scalabrini was performing the religious ceremony for the said departure of Sisters and Missionaries, and the songs and the harmonies of the harmonium were therefore resounding, at the same time were heard the tolling that announced the funeral of Alessandro; and when afterward the Sisters and the Missionaries climbed into the carriage bound for the station, the tolling announcing the funeral procession from the Cathedral to the Cemetery was heard. We all felt our hearts tighten at the thought of the anguish of our Mother, but she gave no sign of anything and attended to her business of that morning, encouraging and exhorting the departing Sisters, and also staying on with the Bishop. I know, however, that she wept over the death of her son; not, however, at the deathbed. When, after the son's death, we returned with her to the mother house, she separated from us and shut herself in her room, where we heard her sobbing for perhaps two hours. After this outpouring I do not know that she wept any more over the death of her son.

The son of the Servant of God had not lived very well; the Servant of God followed him with her prayers, and let it be understood that she prayed a great deal for her son. He, when he felt himself worsened, spontaneously asked for the Guardian of the Capuchins, to whom he confessed and, having received the Viaticum, also asked for Extreme Unction. The Parish Priest visited him often. This is why I said earlier that the Servant of God knew him to be in good hands. I must add that Alessandro, though scatterbrained, had a great heart for the Mother and would have done anything for her.

§ 420
Relations of the Servant of God with her daughter and the latter's family.

Now let us return to the daughter of the Servant of God and her family. I have heard it said that at the beginning the Servant of God had a great esteem for her son-in-law, who showed a certain zeal and helped the Servant of God in extraordinary affairs, but I could not point to special facts. I remember that the Servant of God entrusted to him for three years the administration of the Gargatano. A very widespread rumor among Sisters and lay people said that Barbiellini administered the Gargatano not very honestly, and the Servant of God had the accounts examined by Atty. Bonfiglio, and then took over the administration, which her son-in-law renounced. Also Gaspare's brother, Count Edoardo Barbiellini, played a dirty trick on the Servant of God, and I myself fell for it. In this house there was the general storeroom for the black cloth that clothes our Sisters, and we supplied ourselves from a certain firm, Rossi of Milan. The middleman for these payments was precisely Count Edoardo, who, I do not know how, had received this commission from our Mother. At each presentation of receipts the Mother paid the said Count regularly, and I had the receipts in my keeping, and seeing the payment marked with a revenue stamp I was at ease. But one fine day behold there arrives from the firm Rossi an energetic demand for payment of ten or eleven thousand lire (in this sum, however, it seems to me there was also included a debt to another firm not paid by Count Edoardo). At this demand I pointed out to the Mother that we had our receipts, and in this sense I answered the firm, inviting it to send its representative, to whom we would show the regular receipts. But what was my surprise when, on his coming, he did not recognize the signatures as his. They were forged by Count Edoardo! The Servant of God put the matter in the hands of Atty. Pediconi, who wanted to seize the furniture of the said Edoardo, because he possessed nothing else. Edoardo asked forgiveness, begged and implored, but the Mother showed herself inflexible; in the end, however, she yielded to my plea not to seize it and to be content with bills of exchange at term. It is understood that these bills were never paid to her.

These matters of so delicate a kind I wish to be kept secret even after the process.

Proc. fol. 2135v.: Returning to Count Gaspare Barbiellini, I know that the Servant of God had also given him a general power of attorney, but that, noticing his lack of correctness, she withdrew it from him by act of the Notary Monti, I think after the administration of the Gargatano had been settled. I know from other Sisters that the son-in-law and the daughter continually tormented the Servant of God to get money or something else.

I have heard it told, I think by Benedetta Carrega and also by Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, that once her daughter Carlotta, who was insisting with the Servant of God to have I do not know what, she gently refused, answering that what she could give her she had given her, and that she was poor and could not give things belonging to the Institute. Then the daughter threatened to throw herself from the window. The Servant of God was much moved, and I know no more. Except that, according to the Sisters, that was a ruse to wring from the Mother what she desired.

§ 421
Communication between the houses of Rome and Piacenza and the relatives' houses.

I have heard it said by the Sisters and by Fr. Agostino Donadio that by the brothers of the Servant of God the small villa to the right of this Generalate House was built, assigning the ground floor to her brother Federico, the first floor to the daughter of the Servant of God, and the second to her son Alessandro, should he come, and to her brother Francesco; and that, the mother of the Servant of God having died in that time, she said: «Well then, this money that now comes to me from the family, I shall use in this house for my children».

p. 255

At the beginning, when the masons were still working, there was an internal communication between this house and theirs, but when the works were completely finished, it was closed; and before they finished, the relatives were already there.

Also next to our Mother House at Piacenza the son-in-law bought himself a House, separated from ours by a vegetable garden. When the Novitiate at Piacenza was then built, there was an internal communication between it and the Barbiellini House, which, however, was closed, I do not remember after how long, by the Servant of God herself, at least so it seems to me. There was a communication between the two gardens of the two houses, and this, it seems to me, remained. The supervision of the construction of the Novitiate at Piacenza was held by Gaspare Barbiellini, and I have heard it said by the Sisters that in this too he was not correct, but I cannot specify anything.

The Holy Father Leo XIII, through Cardinal Alimonda, Protector of the Institute, let the Servant of God know that he desired the Generalate House of our Institute to be in Rome, because he saw that the Institute was spreading; but the Servant of God had no money and, wishing nevertheless to comply with the Holy Father's will, turned to her brothers for help. These agreed, although the sister, when they spoke to her about it, had in her pocket only thirty centesimi, as I have heard; and from the Banca Tiberina the area of our Convent and of the Small Villa Gattorno on the right was bought, her brother Francesco and Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega standing surety with their signature.

The construction of this our House was almost finished when Francesco fell ill with pleurisy, and then the area was divided and the accounts settled. Mr. Francesco showed himself most honest, as always, on this occasion too. In this construction of our Generalate House Count Barbiellini had no part at all, to his displeasure.

The little nephews and nieces of the Servant of God with their mamma came almost every day to the house, but at an hour mostly when we were at table or at recreation. The Servant of God, as soon as she had finished eating, went out and stayed with them mostly in the study, and a few rare times in the garden. I noticed that the Servant of God was sometimes distressed, and I heard her say: «Oh what a cross! But on the other hand what am I to do?».

§ 422
Dignified reaction of the Servant of God to the Apostolic Visitation.

Ad 25, Proc. fol. 2143v.: Because of various appeals that were made to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, the Apostolic Visitation of this our Institute was ordered. In these appeals, as I have heard it said, Count Gaspare Barbiellini had a great part, and it is claimed also some of our Sisters; but of anything concrete I could say nothing.

We were at Piacenza, Mother Gattorno, I, then her Assistant, Mother Carrega, and I do not remember whether the other two Assistants, Sr. A. Camilla Valentini and Sr. A. Teresa Sorrentino, were also there, when the Apostolic Visitor arrived suddenly, the Benedictine Abbot General, today Cardinal Serafini, with his brother Dom Mauro, as Secretary. The Servant of God was called to the parlor, and believed it was a matter of other business, and was surprised when she learned the purpose of that coming of Abbot Serafini, since she had had no advance notice from anyone, not even from the Cardinal Protector. The Visitor said to her straight out: «As you will know, I come in the name of the Holy See». And the Servant of God: «But truly I know nothing». And the Visitor: «But did the Cardinal Protector not warn you?». «No — she resumed. — Oh! at last! It was so long that people had been speaking of this Apostolic Visitation. The moment has come at last when what God has done in His Work will be known». I believe that the Servant of God had already been forewarned supernaturally of this Apostolic Visitation, as certain expressions that escaped her, and also other Sisters intimate with the Servant of God, such as Mother Carrega and Sr. Teresa Maria Sorrentino, made me reflect after the fact: expressions, however, that I now could not determine.

Concerning those expressions, I now recall that once the Servant of God said clearly these words: «Oh, what will ever befall the work of God!». And this before the Apostolic Visitation. I do not remember whether, in presenting us Sisters to the Visitor, in presenting Mother Carrega to him, she put before her name her title of Marchioness. This, however, I know: that when she presented her to outsiders, she sometimes put it before; she did not permit, however, that among the Sisters they be called by their title.

Having learned the purpose of that Visitation, the Servant of God said: «Here I am, I am ready». I was filled with admiration at the ease of the Servant of God, who showed herself ready at the nods and wishes of the Visitor, and of that first moment I recall nothing more.

p. 257

The Visitor saw, examined little by little a great part of our Houses of the Institute in Italy. I know that the Servant of God forewarned the Provincials and the principal Superiors of this Apostolic Visitation, but only in general.

She said: «The Apostolic Visitor is above me: now we must be subject to him, and what he does is well done: I can do nothing any more».

When the Visitation at Piacenza was finished, the Visitor said to the Servant of God: «You continue your government until October (we were then at the end of July 1898), and then we shall see. You will make no new foundations of houses without informing me». And he made another prescription which I no longer remember. The Servant of God warned the Sisters that, if any were not obedient to the Visitor, she could not receive Communion.

Now I recall the other prescription the Visitor made, and it was not to dismiss any Sister with perpetual Vows without first consulting him. This, truly, had never been done before, as the Servant of God pointed out to the Visitor.

I know that the Visitor paid the Servant of God compliments on various Houses. In general he showed himself rather satisfied. The Servant of God, when she had heard the praises, would then say to us: «The work is not mine, but the Crucified One's».

I always saw the Servant of God full of respect toward the Visitor, because he, she said, is the one who now commands.

Ad 26: It seems to me that there is no need even to speak of the Servant of God's observance of the commandments of God and of the Church, even in small things. She likewise scrupulously observed all the obligations of her various states; she observed, and had her Sisters minutely observe, the rules of her Institute.

Ad 27: The Servant of God possessed and practiced all the Theological virtues, as well as the Cardinal ones and the others connected with them.

§ 423
Living faith of the Servant of God from infancy until death.

The Servant of God always told us that God had set faith in her like a diamond, so alive and deep did she feel it. I heard her say: «Oh, if it were given me to shed my blood for the faith!». The talk of the Servant of God in her exhortations, in her conferences, was always this: to stand strong in the faith and attached to the Holy See. If anyone had allowed himself some criticism of the Pope, she interrupted, declaring that she did not want to hear it, because, where the Pope is concerned, all is well; no criticism or opposition is to be admitted.

As a young girl, going into the country with her family, she gathered the peasants' girls to instruct them in the things of the faith. And this she always did until she passed to marriage.

Then, as a widow, she took part in all the Catholic associations in Genoa, and in a particular way in the Daughters of Mary, of which she was President, as I heard from herself. She had, she told us too, created groups in the various centers of the Daughters of Mary, and from time to time she gathered the Presidents of these groups to give them a conference on the Catechism, on the way to guide the Daughters of Mary and to make piety and all the virtues grow in them. The teaching of the catechism she always inculcated on all the Superiors, and on me, when I was at the Parrocchietta; and so too she recommended the instruction and assistance of the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary; and in this Generalate House she wished one to be founded, in which she took the greatest interest, so that they might be well instructed, so that they might have a good Director who would cultivate them well in the spirit. She provided them with little gifts, she went down to see them. She took an interest in the first Communions of boys and girls in the Church of this House. She recommended to the Sisters that they also look after the little boys, up to six or seven years, and no more.

§ 424
A woman of prayer and deep meditation.

Proc. fol. 2153: How much the Servant of God prayed! Besides her meditation in the morning, at Piacenza in the free hours she went up to her little secret room, and there she prayed, as could be understood very well from her expressions, such as these: «Oh! I go up there to recollect myself and to lift myself up a little!». And when she came down, you should have seen her, how radiant she was; she had a face of Paradise; and I was quite happy when I knew that she withdrew or had withdrawn to her cell, because I would then have the pleasure of contemplating her face, which infused something heavenly into my soul.

At night, as she declared, she slept little, and «I spend my hours in prayer and meditation», she added to us.

Here in Rome, when she had some free hour, she went to the Chapel and sometimes locked herself in there so as not to be disturbed. In the last years, notwithstanding her sufferings, she was with her thoughts more there than here. For me her union with God was continual, and this union of hers appeared manifest even to those who came to visit her. They were all enchanted to find themselves before this person all humble, who spoke little and was all submissive. When they went out, they said to us: «Oh what a Mother you have!», and gave us to understand that they had conceived an esteem for her as of an extraordinary woman.

Mostly the Servant of God, when she prayed, knelt with one arm resting on the chair, never moving; and she was so absorbed that we refrained from disturbing her when we saw her so recollected. Once the Bishop of La Paz (in Bolivia) came to celebrate Mass in the Chapel, and the Servant of God, with all of us, received Holy Communion from his hands. There is in Bolivia this custom: when the Celebrant is about to recite the last Gospel, the Missal is carried to be kissed by the person for whom the Mass is being celebrated. And on this occasion the Bishop's Secretary or Assistant, taking the Missal, carried it to the Servant of God to kiss, but did not succeed; and the Bishop himself understood so well that she was all absorbed in God that he ordered that she be disturbed no more. I was present.

§ 425
Most devoted to the Crucified.

Proc. fol. 2176: She was most devoted to the Crucified.
