She herself told us that while still living with her family, as a widow, one evening, praying before a Crucifix, she saw it fall from the Cross, and she then put it back on its Cross, nailing it. The following evening the same thing happened again, and she again nailed it. On the third evening again the Crucifix came off the Cross; then, believing herself not capable, she handed it to her maidservant to see to nailing it well: and she (a certain Manin, now deceased) — I do not know well whether she herself nailed it or had someone else nail it — then returned it to the Servant of God, who on the fourth evening saw it fall again before her, as she prayed. The Servant of God was then impressed, and understood and said to the Lord: «You want, then, that I carry the Cross». And she nailed it no more.

The Servant of God told us that the Cross must not be dragged, but clasped to the breast; and when she had some tribulation (which never failed her), pressing her arms crossed on her breast, she said: «Yes, O Jesus, you have given it to me and I clasp it to my bosom».

p. 260

§ 426
A grace attributed to the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 2192v.: Sr. Anna Gasparina Catalanotto, now Superior at Lucera, I do not remember well whether still a Novice, obtained through the Servant of God this grace. She fell ill in one arm and, for all the care they gave her, and for all that Doctor Montechiari did, nothing was achieved but to make it worsen and swell more and more. The Superior of this House, Sr. Anna Solenghi, came to the Servant of God all alarmed to explain the case to her. And she answered: «Bring the sick one to me here» (because, owing to her sufferings that day, she was not in a condition to move). And when the sick one was brought, the Servant of God, as usual, said: «It is nothing», although I, who was present, was frightened at seeing the arm so swollen. She made the sign over her with her wood of the Holy Cross and sent her back to the infirmary, saying to her: «There must be nothing more». Sr. Anna Gasparina, as soon as she was signed by the Servant of God, felt better, and the same day improved so much that she had no more need of doctors or of medicines. I know that this Sister received other favors of the same kind from the Servant of God, but I could not tell them.

I know that many and many other graces the Servant of God worked with her wood of the Holy Cross, which now I could not recount because I do not remember.

§ 427
Two crosses used as instruments of penance.

When we entered her secret room at Piacenza, after her death, we found two thick pieces of wood put together in the form of a cross, tied with well-ropes, which we could not manage to understand how the Servant of God had carried up. To the arms of the Cross were tied two iron hooks, and on the lower part of the Cross two iron footrests likewise tied to the Cross, and it appeared evidently that the Servant of God stretched herself upon it in the manner of the Cross itself, the hooks at the arms of the Cross serving to support her own. This Cross we found leaning against a corner of the wall. We also found on one arm of the Cross a large rosary of fifteen decades, such as to make us suppose that she, stretching herself on the Cross, said the Rosary.

We found another Cross, much smaller, placed on two little benches.

She was truly the lover of the Cross!

§ 428
Visit of the Servant of God to the shrines of Our Lady.

Proc. fol. 2212: Almost all her journeys the Servant of God ended with a visit to some Shrine of Our Lady. To that of Loreto alone I accompanied her four times at the end of her journeys; and I saw her motionless for hours and hours in prayer, so that Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega and I grew tired and went out of the Holy House to go and sit. All the free time in those two or three days in which we stayed, she spent there in the Holy House, as if in ecstasy. I myself accompanied her once to the Shrine of Oropa, where she hoped to convert her brother Federico. Once I accompanied her to the Shrine of Pompeii, and another time to Lourdes. There too, in those three or four days that we stayed, all the time she had free she spent in prayer, kneeling on the ground.

§ 429
Trust of the Servant of God in the Lord.

Proc. fol. 2255: As to Hope, I heard the Servant of God speak with much confidence of going to Paradise, and say expressions full of conviction.

Sometimes, looking at the difficulties in which the Institute found itself in the first years, in which I was in the Secretariat, I said to the Servant of God: «But you, Mother, when you go to bed, will you not be able to sleep?». «Oh no! my daughter — she answered me — when I retire to my room in the evening, I think for two minutes, and then I turn to my Crucifix and say to him: “I have done everything I could and in the best way I could; you think now of your work”, and I lay everything then at the feet of my Crucifix, and I think no more of it, as if the work did not exist». And these expressions I heard repeated also to various Superiors.

In her expressions of confidence of going to Paradise she showed that the basis of this confidence of hers was the merits of Blessed Jesus. Writing to the Superiors, she exhorted them to bear in peace, with holy resignation, the crosses that the Lord sent them, in the trust of the eternal reward.

§ 430
Filial trust and resignation in difficult moments.

Many times I was edified at seeing her bear her crosses with patience. The Servant of God used to tell that, when she was left a widow, her father-in-law refused to give the little grandchildren the share due; wherefore her father had to bring suit against the father-in-law. Naturally there were not lacking in this affair sorrows, but she felt calm, as if it were nothing, and so calm that her father, amazed, asked her: «But what have you in your veins, Annina, blood or water?». And she answered that there would be someone who would help her and take her part.

In January or February of 1891, while we were at Piacenza with the Servant of God, she received news that our Sisters of Prato and Pistoia, three of the one and three of the other House, had separated from our Institute to make a new foundation. At that time the Servant of God was assisting her son Alessandro by order of Mgr. Scalabrini. The Servant of God was much embarrassed, and said: «But what to do now? If only I had someone to send!». And to relieve her of that embarrassment I offered myself, if I were good for something; and then she sent me. I went, but did not succeed in avoiding the fact of the schism already accomplished. Returned to Piacenza to report to the Servant of God what had happened, she said to me with complete calm: «See here, I have already received a telegram, which reports to me the defection of these Sisters». I added that they had already carried off the linen, books, and all that they could. But she was not disturbed, and said: «The harm they have done to themselves. The work will not suffer from it: my Crucifix will see to it». Her peace and calm made a great impression on me.

In April 1900 one day the Servant of God comes into the study while I was alone; she sits down and leans on the table, because her illness pulled her down greatly. At that time I was very worried about the future of the Institute. I saw that soon we should no longer have our venerated Mother; I foresaw the assaults that the Barbiellini family would give us, and I was turning a thousand things over in my brain. When the Servant of God had sat down, I asked her whether I might have a little soup brought to her, and, she having assented, I had it brought. While she, bent over the plate, was taking that soup, I, seated beside her, my head resting on one hand so that she should not see, was weeping, ever at the sight of the difficulties into which shortly I saw the Institute plunged. All at once I hear the Servant of God murmuring, still bent over her plate; I listen and hear that she says: «Be calm; all will go well; have trust». «Yes, I am calm, O Mother — I answer her — but I weep because I see you suffer so much. These ills should surely be enough». Then the Servant of God, laying her cutlery on the plate, turns to me, drawing herself up and with her hand on her breast says to me: «You are not calm at all, and if I tell you so it is because I know it, and you cannot deny it to me. Be calm, then, I repeat to you, for all will go well; I have been assured that in the Secretariat all is in order, and no one will ever be able to touch a hair of your heads. And if I tell you this, it is because I know it: at the gates is my Salvatore, who will protect you». Her Salvatore would be Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi, who died in June 1885 in the odor of sanctity, and of whom the Process has already been begun at Palermo. At these words of the Servant of God I burst the more into tears, and at a good moment Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega arrived with the daughter of the Servant of God, Carlotta. The Servant of God with those words read my inner heart, and they were a true prophecy, for the Barbiellini in the last days, indeed during the agony of the Servant of God, were plotting to have the seals put everywhere, but notwithstanding this, and notwithstanding ten years of litigation, they could do us no harm, and touch nothing.

§ 431
Out of love of God she avoided even the lightest faults.

Proc. fol. 2275v.: As to the charity of the Servant of God, I am certain that she tried to avoid even the lightest faults. She greatly inculcated the observance of the rules, even in small things, because, she said, «the devil does not tempt in great things, but in small things, so as then to make his way to the great ones». «When you have a little free time — she told us — instead of wasting time in idle words, go to Jesus, and be thieves. Steal, steal». I could not name the slightest fault that I noticed in her.

She suffered much if she saw silence not well observed; if she knew that in some community there was not perfect regular observance, she reproved. Having learned that in one Community there was not much recollection, by way of penance, as appears from a letter, she obliged them always to speak in a low voice for a week.

Proc. fol. 2297: Before going further in my deposition, I shall say still, concerning the devotion of the Servant of God to St. Anne, that she would have wished to found a new Institute of the Sons of St. Anne. Directed by the Servant of God, Cardinal di Belmonte, then very young, had agreed with five or six other personages, among whom I seem to recall Mgr. Bonito, a certain Leotti, Professor Amirante, a project for the said foundation, which should have been of help for the direction of the Daughters of St. Anne, and coming to Rome, I think in 1888, he presented it to the Holy Father, who, however, did not give a favorable opinion, and so nothing came of it.

So also the Servant of God brought about an Institute of Tertiaries of St. Anne.

Mgr. Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, had in the City a Home for deaf-mute girls, entrusted to the Daughters of Charity of St. Vincent. About 1884, one day he came to propose to the Servant of God that she entrust to her Sisters the home in question, manifesting together the project of founding in that Home an Institute of Tertiaries of St. Anne, who would have the purpose of Adoration of the Most Blessed Sacrament. And so it was done.

§ 432
Horror of the Servant of God at sin.

Mgr. Scalabrini wished the new Sisters to have our same rule and to remain under our direction. The Servant of God made sacrifices for the foundation, and Mgr. Scalabrini ceded to the Institute the house in the City and the one in the country.

The Servant of God felt horror of every sin. I myself heard her exclaim many times: «By the grace of God no, no, mortal sin has never entered into her work, and of this I can hold my head high. Yes, it is true that someone has prevaricated, but the Holy Mother rejected her in time. If I knew that sin entered into the work of the Lord, I would die of grief».

When the Servant of God heard that there were rallies and agitations against the Church of God, she had the Blessed Sacrament exposed in the Chapel and wanted all the Sisters to go and adore it.

§ 433
Apostolate of catechism out of charity toward neighbor.

Proc. fol. 2307v.: As to charity toward the Neighbor, and beginning with the spiritual works, I shall say that the Servant of God, even from when she was in the world, concerned herself with Catechism; then, when she was in the Institute, she did it personally for the little girls; then, hindered by her office of General, she recommended to her Sisters the catechetical instruction of children, both by word and in writing. As to the letters, her interest in Catechism shows itself much in them, especially in the letters to the first Sisters. For the rest, it is revealed also afterward. She was a woman of great counsel; and we have in the Secretariat many letters of the Sisters which attest that they owe their vocation to the counsels of the Servant of God.

An altar boy of ours at Piacenza, having shown a wish to become a priest, was at once helped by the Servant of God to be received and maintained in the Seminary of Mgr. Masnini. After some time it seemed to the Servant of God that that young lad was not called to the Ecclesiastical state, and then she declared to him that what she was spending for him she must employ in other good works. That young lad, seeing such protection and help fail him, came one day to the Servant of God, and I remember having seen him myself in her study kneeling before the Mother, begging and imploring her to maintain her help to him, and making her a thousand promises. But to all his entreaties the Servant of God replied: «No, do me the favor, give up this habit; you are not called to be a Priest; look for a good job, and you will be a good layman». Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, however, was moved, to whom the Mother's resistance seemed hardness, and she said to the Mother: «What you do not wish to do, do you permit me to do?». And the permission asked having been obtained, the young lad was placed in the Episcopal Seminary. After some time, however, a letter of the young lad himself addressed to Sr. A. Benedetta informed her that he did not feel up to going on in the ecclesiastical career. Carrega, informing the Mother of this afterward, was answered: «But do you think I would have resisted so much if I had not been sure that he had no vocation?».

§ 434
In many ways she manifested charity toward her neighbor.

Proc. fol. 2313: I have heard it told by the older Sisters that the Servant of God, when as a lay woman she went to the Hospital of Pammatone, reserved for herself the most tiresome patients and those most obstinate in matters of religion. So likewise in the Hospital of Cento, which was the first accepted by her.

When some Sister had failed, the Servant of God reproved her calmly, making her note the harm done to her soul and to the Institute. For repeated offenses she showed herself a little more severe.

Besides what I have said of her concern for her brothers, I can add that this extended also to her other relatives, when she saw them not so concerned about matters of religion.

She was ready, however, to forget the failings of all, men and women, saying that we are all frail. I can say with all certainty that she was ready to forget the failings and offenses done to her Institute, and that she received persons who had offended her as if nothing had happened.

When she noticed that among some of her Sisters there was some small disagreement, she observed, kept silent, and with one word arranged everything.

§ 435
Love toward those who did not esteem her, and consoler of the afflicted.

She was most tolerant of troublesome persons; and even if she knew that some Sister of hers did not have a great esteem for her, it was as if nothing had happened. I remember that with a Superior in America she always behaved with very good letters, while the latter always answered a little harshly; and she said: «I want to win her with kindness». There were naturally tiresome Sisters, but she bore them with great ease.

When she knew that a Sister had had a misfortune in her family, or that something adverse had happened to her, she called her to herself and consoled her with kind words and did not leave her until she had calmed down, and in general she obtained the desired effect.

As long as she was in a condition to be able to do so, she went to console the families of benefactors struck by some calamity.

Having then come to Rome, she established that every Saturday fifty kilos of bread be given to the poor at our door. Likewise, that at Christmas, Easter, and Shrove Thursday they might have a little macaroni with sausages.

Receiving requests from poor families, she sent to verify, and finding the account true, she helped them. I also know that she gave secret alms to impoverished and shamefaced families.

§ 436
Charity toward the sick.

She visited her sick Sisters even at night, and when no one noticed. I remember that Sr. A. Candida Quadrani, Superior of the Deaf-Mutes at Piacenza, once fell ill with a gastro-verminous colic, which Doctor Montechiari judged very dangerous. The Servant of God paid her a visit at one o'clock after midnight, blessed her in her own way, and said to her: «Tomorrow morning get up, and go to the refectory with the others, and speak no more of illness, for there is nothing wrong any more». And so it was; the next day Sr. Candida got up and had nothing any more. So I heard from Sr. Candida herself.

§ 437
Out of prudence she spoke little and in a measured way.

Proc. fol. 2374v.: The Servant of God was very prudent, spoke little and measured, with a grave and concentrated bearing. She was very discreet, and when someone confided something to her, there was no chance that she would let anything leak out.

When she received letters of praise and commendation for herself or for her work, she said: «These are things that do not concern us; the work is the Lord's». I recall that a certain gentleman one day said to me and to Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega words of commendation for our Institute, and revealed the fine qualities of our Mother. I was greatly gladdened by it, and in the evening, accompanying the Servant of God to her room, I had the imprudence to say to her: «Mother, but do you not know that this and that is said of you?». And she: «Oh! my poor daughter! What are you saying? The work is the Lord's, I am nothing but his donkey». And these words she said with such sincerity and frankness that I was edified.

§ 438
She recommended kindness in corrections.

Seeing that various Superiors exceeded in the correction of the Sisters, she gathered them in exercises, if I am not mistaken in 1886 and in 1888, and in one of her usual conferences held with them she proposed various cases (her notes having been written down), asking them: «in this or that case, what would a Superior deserve who acted in such a way?». And thus she came to establish certain norms of punishment for the Superiors who had exceeded in corrections, which were of great benefit. I acted at that time as Secretary to take the notes, which were afterward printed, and some copy is kept, and I present to the Holy Tribunal a copy of those printed norms.

When she sent the visitors to the houses, she recommended to them above all the care of the sick. I never heard nor learned from Sisters that she ever allowed herself frivolous or idle words.

§ 439
She asked for prayers and counsel in grave cases.

When she had something important to decide, she greatly recommended us to pray; in those days we saw her more recollected than usual, and she made more use than usual of spare moments to go to the chapel or to her room. In the graver cases she also had the Blessed Sacrament exposed for some hours of the day and sent us to pray.

In the more important matters she took counsel with prudent persons, such as Fr. Bernardino of Portogruaro and, when he was no longer in Rome, with Mgr. di Belmonte, now Cardinal, and for daily and ordinary matters with Fr. Agostino Donadio. I have also heard it said that in the first years she took much counsel with Fr. Tornatore, Priest of the Mission. I do not know why she no longer made use of him, or at least I did not notice, because I no longer saw that intimacy of which I had been told.

It is her example that taught us to hold the generalate councils and the other chapters for the more important matters. There still exist in the Secretariat the minutes of the meetings with her signature.

§ 440
She gave everyone what was just and expressed her gratitude to benefactors.

As to justice, I shall say first of all that with workmen she did not haggle, and gave them what was just. She examined the accounts of the House, and if she found them a little exaggerated she called the local Superior, and I too was present at some remark she made to her.

If she came to know that some parent of a Sister was in bad condition, she came to their help.

If some Sister showed herself of more special virtue and of greater spirit of sacrifice, such as Sr. Anna Salvatore Orsi, she had some regard. Sr. Anna Salvatore too, however, had her trials at first; but then, when it was known who Sr. A. Salvatore was, then the regard began. Of this one I have heard it said that she kept vigil through the nights in prayer, and I have also heard it said that in this House no, because the chapel was distant from her room, she would have been noticed, but in the house at Piacenza she went out softly at night, when we had retired, and went to the little choir gallery. It must be noted that today, that little choir gallery having been raised by Mother Carrega, there is no longer access to it from the Mother's little secret room.

The Servant of God was most grateful to those who did her some favor, and I would say even too much so.

She established a special daily prayer to be recited every day for benefactors in general.

For Countess Caracciolo, a great benefactress of our Institute in the beginning, the Servant of God sacrificed herself much during the time of her illness, always assisting her.

§ 441
Always mortified, even when traveling.

The Servant of God was mortified in her eyes. When she went on the train, she did not care to look at or observe anything. Traveling, she was accustomed to take out a quantity of rosaries, put on her spectacles, open the little book of common prayers, and so pass a long time; and she remained absorbed in her prayers, interrupted only by the greetings of her Daughters at the various stations. Since I traveled with her, I found that she suffered much, very much.

The food of the Servant of God in the morning was a cup of black coffee without sugar. At midday a little meatless soup, then preferably a dish of salt cod, then potatoes or greens or legumes. I never saw her eat meat, nor drink wine. In the last years, however, a little white wine was imposed on her. A little milk was sometimes ordered for her; out of obedience she adapted to it, but then had to leave it. She sometimes adapted to taking an egg, because Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega insisted, but her great aversion was noticeable.

In the evening her food was another little soup, and ordinarily a dish of legumes or greens; rarely a little fish, and apart from salt cod other fish was little to her liking. It became known that she was very fond of cured pork sausage; and I heard her say that as a child she went to the family pantry, cut a thick slice of salami and ate it.

On solemn feast days, when she was a Religious, salami, cotichino, or zampone being distributed to the Community, she went herself to the kitchen to cut it and make the portions, which she made abundant and wanted everyone to eat; so we saw how she, stirring up her old desire, mortified herself.

§ 442
Fortitude in following her vocation and in the foundation of the Institute.

Proc. fol. 2393v.: Her fortitude shone in leaving her family, as I have said. Knowing her mother gravely ill, she went to visit her at Genoa, but then, called urgently to Rome, going to the station, she passed under the window of her dying mother, and felt her heart break, as she herself confessed to us, but she did not go up the stairs, and went on, receiving afterward the telegram of her mother's death as she passed through Pisa.

She herself told us that in the very beginnings of the Institute, struggling amid a thousand financial difficulties, and also because there were those who did not look on the Institute with a kindly eye, a priest presented himself to say to her: «But what are you doing here? Close up shop and all of you go home, it is better». And she answered that, despite all the difficulties, since it was the work of God, she had to continue, and that Pius IX had told her that it would last until the end of the world.

§ 443
Unyielding before unjust bullies.

She did not yield before the high-handedness of administrators of works entrusted to her, and when the honor and decorum of the Institute had to be upheld. I recall that at Rossano, I think, the administrators of the Hospital wanted to rescind the contract with us, spreading facts not pleasant for us. The Servant of God put the matter in the hands of a Lawyer, and made the administrators keep to their place. I recall other facts only confusedly, which therefore I could not recount.

In the ordinary way, however, the Servant of God said: «Let us shake our sandals and withdraw».

When one, because of poor health, was obliged to withdraw from teaching, she made use of her diploma to bring in another Sister, capable indeed but without a diploma, so as to be able to do a little good and to avoid the substitution of a lay Teacher, and this too was approved by the Royal School Superintendent.

The Servant of God was always suffering in body, but always resigned; and, as I heard from the old Sisters, she found herself in this state from the beginning of the Institute; and she was not only always resigned, but always very active.

§ 444
She was most delicate in the exercise of chastity.

As to Chastity, besides what can be drawn from what has been said so far in my deposition, I recall that when she went out, if she heard some little word not good, she at once made the sign of the cross.

I never heard her speak of her marriage, and when she recalled her husband she used to call him Carlotta's Papa.

As to obedience, I shall say that it is seen from the letters written by her Confessor at Genoa, when she was still in the world, and which we found after her death, that she was perfectly submissive to him.

§ 445
Blind and total obedience to superiors.

I remember having heard it told by Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, Superior of the House of Siena, that, finding herself one day with the Mother, Tornatore being present, in the first times of the Institute, she noticed that the Mother was suffering, because she was laden with hairshirts and little chains, and that at a given moment the Mother said to Tornatore in a low voice: «I can bear no more»; and that Fr. Tornatore said to her: «Take them off for five minutes». And she withdrew.

Sometimes these expressions escaped her: «This must be done, because it has been ordered me».

She was very submissive to the Cardinal Protectors; and when she returned from her visits to the Houses, she gave an immediate report to the Cardinal Protector. And I remember that once, as soon as her journeys were finished, she went directly to Turin to the Cardinal Protector Alimonda. The Servant of God was also deferential to us in observations and counsels.

§ 446
Poverty effective and affective in everything.

As to her poverty, it remains for me to speak only of her rooms. Of the one at Piacenza I have already spoken. The furnishing of this one in Rome consists of a straw mattress, two small tables and a few chairs, as can still be seen today. The washstand here in Rome was of iron; she used laundry soap and did not tolerate toilet soap, not even for the Sisters. Woe if, when she went on visitation, the Superiors offered her bars of soap!

The somewhat decorous furnishing of our guesthouse cost six thousand lire, if I remember well, and was a gift of a former Dominican, a certain Fr. Benedetto, very rich. He had already shown himself very generous also for our house at Prato, and the Superior had turned to him at the suggestion of Mgr. Franchi, then Vicar General and afterward Bishop of Livorno. The Servant of God complained about this guesthouse of ours, it seeming to her too luxurious, but she had had nothing to do with it, because it was the Benefactor who took care of the purchase directly. As to the material part of the entrance, that is, marble stairs, etc., I recall that when the Servant of God was invited to come and see the works, which were already well advanced, the Servant of God, when she was in the first parlor, let her veil fall and, putting her hands on her hips, turning to her brother Francesco, in a tone of reproach, said to him: «But what have you done to me, Checco? It looks to me like a Hotel!». And he answered her in her ear: «Let it be; they will no longer call you a ragamuffin». Truly, at that time we were called ragamuffins. I was present at this episode.

It is my opinion that the Servant of God sometimes called her Sisters by the noble title they had in the world when presenting them to outsiders, precisely to relieve the Institute of the name of ragamuffin Sisters which it had in the early times.

§ 447
Humility: she did not like honorific titles.

Proc. fol. 2400: Humility. The Servant of God had a low opinion of herself. When she spoke of herself she always said that she was a poor ragamuffin, a donkey, and when she wanted to say something very noble of herself, she said that she was a poor slave of her Crucifix, and these expressions she said with an accent of true conviction, she did not admit praise concerning herself, and all this I know. If her Institute was praised, she referred everything to the Lord, and if she felt some complacency, it was all out of regard for her Crucifix. She was much annoyed if some Sister, writing to her, put on the address «Mother General»; she grieved still more if she was called Foundress, and that Sister had to be warned; and when she told us of the Secretariat to warn those Sisters, she added: «Your Mother yes, but as to the title of General, let us leave it to those who have merit», and that she was not Foundress of the Institute, which, if it had a Founder, this was Pius IX.

Once the Servant of God, as I heard from herself, found a booklet of memoirs about herself and the Institute written by her first Secretary, Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino; she took it and burned it.

Once, visiting the houses of Sicily, Mother Carrega and I accompanied the Servant of God to Cardinal Dusmet, Archbishop of Catania. She went in alone to the Cardinal, with whom she remained in a very long conversation, and coming out she showed herself indifferent with us. She only said to us after a while: «We shall have to withdraw from that House». She then settled all her affairs and withdrew the Sisters. Of that conversation we knew nothing, except this which was later reported to us by Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, Provincial of Sicily, now deceased; to whom Cardinal Dusmet, speaking of that conversation, said: «I was edified by the humility and submission of your Mother, for however much I said to her, and I said many things to her, she took it all in holy peace».

I heard from Mother Carrega, and I was not then in the Secretariat, that there was a time when the Servant of God no longer wished to be General, but that, she having gone with the Secretary Mother Carrega in audience to the Holy Father Leo, when the Pope learned that she wished to withdraw, he said to her: «Ah no, rather I appoint you for life». And so in our General Chapters her name was no longer put to the vote.

§ 448
Out of humility she tried not to be photographed.

Princess Trotti of Ferrara, desiring greatly to have a portrait of the Servant of God, advised her to have herself portrayed, but she resisted all pressures, and the Princess resorted to having a photograph taken of her secretly and by surprise, which however turned out badly, and I do not know it.

In 1878 the Servant of God sent to La Paz in Bolivia the first daughters, having them accompanied by Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, her companion of clothing. As is natural, Sr. Giuseppa suffered very much from this separation, and asked the Servant of God for her photograph, she going so far away. The Servant of God was advised to consent, and consented. This is that photograph reproduced in large size, which hangs in our reception hall in this House. I was not then in the Secretariat, and I heard it told by the older Sisters.

In 1893 the Mother began to feel her ailments a little more. Our Sisters in America feared her very ill, and wrote asking for her photograph. Cardinal Verga, Protector, having learned of this request, obliged the Servant of God to satisfy those distant daughters, and committed Mother Carrega to have the photographer come to the house. And so we have the photograph that has been reproduced in the Articles of the Postulator. This did not please the Servant of God, but against her will she had to adapt. At that time I too was in this house with the Mother.

Not only do I believe that the Servant of God persevered, but I am persuaded that she always progressed in the exercise of the Theological, Cardinal and connected Virtues, of which I have spoken. This is the impression that I carried away from the whole of her acts and words, in dealing with her. I also heard our Sisters say: «Our Mother is becoming ever more a Saint».

§ 449
She practiced the virtues in an absolutely extraordinary way.

Ad 28: This is my concept, my conviction: that the degree of all the above-enumerated virtues of the Servant of God was truly heroic, because all were exercised by her not in a manner common even to pious persons, but in an absolutely extraordinary degree, and attainable only by her; in an easy, ready, expeditious manner, as if she possessed another nature; in a degree truly of a Saint of the Altars. This is the conviction that I have and assert.

Ad 30, Proc. fol. 2408: First of all I must note that to the large portrait, which hangs in our reception room, a ray of light was added which was not there before, and this on the advice of Mgr. Cani.

§ 450
Prophetic spirit.

The engineer La Monica, by name, I think, Giuseppe, now deceased, was most devoted and most attached to the Servant of God, and required, when we wrote to him in the name of the Mother, to be addressed as son, and not as Mister, and had a very high esteem for her and said that she was an unsurpassable woman. After the death of the Servant of God he told us that, having come to know the Servant of God, one day he presented to her his two little girls, one of eight or nine years, mild, docile, quiet, calm, and the other of six or seven years, lively, a little jealous, in short of a character perfectly opposite to the first, saying to her: «Of this older one we shall make a little nun»; but the Servant of God answered him: «Oh no! we shall have the younger as a little nun». Events showed the truth of the words of the Servant of God, for the first is an excellent mother of a family, and the younger is a Sister of Charity.

Ad 32, Proc. fol. 2444: I know little of the writings of the Servant of God; but in the little I have read, I have found nothing that is in the least defective and that would not befit a Saint of the Altars; on the contrary I found in them treasures of holiness, which would give scope for other little volumes of golden threads, besides what has already been printed.

§ 451
Last illness and death.

Ad 33: The Servant of God died on 6 May 1900 at 9 in the morning, Consecration of our Church. In my opinion it was from a last attack of a progressive paralysis, of which she had begun to give manifest signs since October 1899, being then on visitation at Genoa. From the first attack she recovered a little and could be transported to Rome, always leaning, as I cannot forget, on my right arm. We had with us Fr. Agostino Donadio, who happened to be at Genoa, and a doctor of Genoa, who was called for fear that the Servant of God could not stand the journey.

Here, with the care of our Doctor Montechiari, she recovered a little more, and I remember that, sitting at her little table, she said: «I have nothing, I own nothing, I have only a few rags, but still I want to make a will». She therefore called the Notary Monti and, consulting with him, made her holograph will, leaving as heirs Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega and me.

§ 452
Will.

This will she then handed to the Notary Monti, not wishing it to remain in our house. And giving the reason for the will she said to us: «I have worked only for my Crucifix, and I want everything to be respected after my death, because the work is his». Then another time I heard her say again in those days: «I have nothing; the will I have made nonetheless, but… who knows whether some signature of mine may not be going around, and whether after my death they may not have it preceded by whatever comes into their heads!». The Notary Monti having therefore been called again, she made a public act, which served us so very much afterward in the Cause we had with the son-in-law of the Servant of God. The will she made in November, and this last act I think she made in the month of April of the following year, 1900.

In the same April Cardinal Rampolla, Protector, came to visit her, and she received him in her study seated on a chair, and was already all swollen. The Cardinal was disturbed, and began to ask her questions about the Institute, how it stood; and I, who was present, remember that the Servant of God, putting her hand on her breast, answered the Cardinal: «Be calm, Eminence, for all is in order, both as to the temporal and as to the spiritual of the Institute, and a child of seven years can go on governing it». And this she repeated many times, at the Cardinal's insistent questions.

§ 453
The sorrows received from her son-in-law aggravated her illnesses.
§ 454
Penitent even on the eve of death.

The sorrows caused by Count Edoardo Barbiellini, of whom I have already spoken (and what I have said I desire to remain most confidential even after the opening of the process), shook her frail health notably and, according to the Doctor, gave her the final blow. The attacks were therefore repeated, and so we came to the third of May. She was always seated on a chair, and refused to sit on an armchair, contenting herself with resting her elbow on the little table. Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega had had the kind thought of having a rush-seated kneeler padded, so that she might have it drawn up easily and lean on it, but not even this did she want. On the third of May, the day of the Holy Cross, she got up, as usual, hoping to continue working, although she fell asleep at work. Incomplete letters were found in her folder, because the Servant of God had interrupted them, falling asleep. Also on the morning of the third of May she worked: at midday she took the usual little meal, but suddenly she felt ill and began to say: «I am dying, I am dying». All of us of the Secretariat, noticing, had the first doctor who could be found sent for, who ordered injections of caffeine, which we proposed to give in a shoulder, but she did not want it, because she did not permit herself to be touched. She already spoke with difficulty. On that same third of May, I and another, supporting her, noticed something that the Servant of God wore at her hips. I therefore told Fr. Agostino Donadio, asking him: «But what has the Mother at her hips? We felt something». And he: «Eh! eh! this is really a bit too much!». And he said nothing else to me. Then the Mother, as I learned at once, called Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia asking her to remove a chain that she wore at her loins, and which, because of the swelling that had afterward come upon her, had sunk entirely into the flesh. Sr. Serafina, naturally, could not remove it; she went in search of pincers, which she obtained from Mother Benedetta Carrega, and with these succeeded in breaking it. Now this chain is kept by us together with other objects that belonged to our Mother.

On the following Friday she worsened greatly. She had a great drowsiness, and we took turns in attending her, also so as not to use up the air in the room. About midday, while we were several Sisters in her room, and as we were going off to lunch, Sr. Benedetta said to me: «While Sr. Serafina stays inside, you stay outside the door, in case the Mother needs something». After a few minutes Sr. Serafina comes out, telling me that the Mother wants to see all the Sisters, and while she runs to call them, I go in; and the Mother says to me, in a manner ever more labored, these words that I could catch: «I have finished suffering; all is averted; the Institute will triumph». And I: «We know well, O Mother, that you offered yourself as victim for the Institute, do not offer yourself any more». And she: «No, no, I shall suffer no more, I have finished; the Institute will triumph: I have averted everything».

Sr. Serafina arrived first, and perhaps understood some of the words of the Servant of God before I spoke; but I am not sure. The other Sisters arrived panting when she was repeating those concepts that I could catch; but perhaps they could not understand, because her speech had become much more inarticulate. From then on I do not know that she spoke any more in an intelligible way.

On the evening of Saturday, the fifth of May, Sr. Benedetta had brought to her the little Madonna of the Ven. Fr. Bernardo Clausi, Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae, and she wished to get up and lean on the table to adore it. Sr. Benedetta Carrega told me that the Servant of God herself had wanted it. I was not there, as I was not there either for the Viaticum, which was given to her that same evening, because my spirit could not bear it.

§ 455
Last spiritual aids of the Church.

I was obliged, however, by Fr. Agostino to bring her the announcement of the blessing that the Holy Father sent her, and I, forcing myself, obeyed. And I remember that at the announcement the eyes of the Servant of God opened, and she smiled at me. I know that immediately afterward Extreme Unction was given to her. At seven or eight o'clock or thereabouts another attack came upon her, and she remained in drowsiness and agony until the moment she rendered her soul to the Lord. And I know no other particulars.

p. 277

In the last moments I went in and out and, precisely at the instant when she expired, I was not present. It was a general weeping.

I forgot to say that in our Chapel there was exposition of the Blessed Sacrament morning and evening in those last days, and that prayer was made in all our Houses with great fervor, and that continual news was requested by telegram from our Provincials.

To St. John Lateran, where the Holy Face of the Savior was exposed, candles and tapers were sent, and many of our Sisters went to pray, and I remember that one day Sr. A. Serafina Foglia came back from there after praying, and told us all sad: «The Mother is dying». We tried to persuade ourselves and her that perhaps she would go on living, but she repeated: «Ah no, no, the Mother is dying».

§ 456
Recommendations before dying.

Ad 34, Proc. fol. 2458: I have heard it said by Sr. A. Serafina Foglia that the Servant of God before dying said to her: «When I am dead, for charity's sake do not abandon me; you see to my corpse, keep me well covered; do not let me be seen by any». And Sr. Serafina truly took care of her corpse; but, not being able to stay alone, because it was all swollen, she had herself helped by three others: by Sr. A. Flora, I think then Mistress of Novices, by Sr. A. Rosella Bolognini, now deceased, and by Sr. A. Consolata Massinelli, then Provincial of Piedmont and now residing at Ovada.

Sr. Serafina told me that she had noticed healed scars on the arms, wrists, hips and above the knees of the Servant of God; in the side she also found a cut three fingers wide, violet in color, which she washed with water and vinegar.

§ 457
Funeral and burial.

The body was laid out in the room where she died until Monday morning, when it was found not only more swollen but in decomposition, and then they hurried to place it in a triple coffin, one of which was of zinc.

It was told me that, when she was laid out, blood came from her mouth. Many people came to see her. Priests and Religious, also of other Institutes, and among the notable persons Mgr. Vincenzo Sardi, now Secretary of the Consistorial. I know that many brought rosaries and other objects of piety close to the body and asked for something of the Servant of God, and that much of her hair was cut and distributed. She had a truly serene and beautiful appearance, so that the said Mgr. Sardi, who had never seen her before, was so sweetly impressed that without difficulty he agreed to deliver the funeral eulogy on the thirtieth day.

In the coffin was placed a tube, I think of glass, with her biographical notes, signed by the General Council. Closed in the coffin, she was carried to our Chapel, where she remained until Tuesday morning, visits continuing always, and then the Apostolic Visitor too, Mgr. Serafini, came to pray before the body. On Tuesday morning she was carried to our Church, where the funeral was held with a great concourse of people, so that the Church was full. In the afternoon, after lunch, she was carried to Campo Verano with a great procession. Of our Sisters alone there must have been about two hundred. Her brothers also attended, but the son-in-law Gaspare saluted the body in Church and went away. The Congregation of the Daughters of Mary was there, from here and that of our school at Prati, with their Directors. There was a representation of the Frascara family, of the Fausti family. The newspapers gave ample accounts of it, which were more or less truthful. In the Cemetery she was laid in our common tomb in the quadrilateral. Then Mother Carrega at once took pains to have the Chapel built at the Pincetto, and here the body was laid on 31 March, if I remember well, 1901, in the presence of several Sisters and a nephew of Mgr. di Belmonte and other lay people, at the door. A notarial act was drawn up by Doctor Tommaso Monti.

§ 458
Conduct of the relatives after the death of the Servant of God.

It was told me (and these things too I wish to remain secret even after the opening of the process) that the granddaughter of the Servant of God, Maria Adelaide, on the night before her grandmother's death, said to her father: «Mind well that as soon as grandmother is dead, you must put your seal on the whole house of the Sisters», and that the father answered her: «Leave it to me: I shall see to it». The Servant of God having died, Sr. Anna Santina Solenghi, perhaps at the suggestion of Mr. Francesco Gattorno, who was present together with Federico, invited Count Gaspare Barbiellini to wait for the Notary Monti in order to do things in order. When he arrived, I do not know what Barbiellini said, because I was not present, but it was reported to me that the Notary said: «Slowly, slowly, Count, because there is a will to be respected». Barbiellini and his daughter Maria became agitated, and demanded outright to see and read the will. «Oh! no! — the Notary resumed — he will take cognizance of it on Tuesday, before the Magistrate, with whom I have made the appointment».

At the suggestion of Mr. Francesco Gattorno a summary inventory of the room of the Servant of God was drawn up at once, to relieve us Sisters of embarrassment. Count Barbiellini, however, did not want to sign it, and went away. A few days later, with the intervention of an Expert and of the aforesaid Notary, a more minute and detailed inventory was drawn up.

I have heard it told that when the first inventory was made, when the wardrobe was opened, the granddaughter Maria Adelaide said that there had been theft, and then, turning to her grandmother, said: «As grandmother I respect you, as General I shall make war on you». And she went away.

Ad 36, Proc. fol. 2464v.: During the exposition of the body there was no forbidden act of cult toward the Servant of God. Going to the Cemetery to visit her body, several years ago, I noticed garlands with the inscription «for G.R.», which at my advice were removed and not put back again. And I know of no other act of undue cult.

§ 459
Fame of holiness.

Ad 38: When the Servant of God died, all our Sisters, as far as I know, said: «A Saint has died», and I always understood that they meant a saint of the Altars. Among persons outside the Institute one heard everyone say: «A great woman has died; a Saint has died»; and so universally was this repeated that Mgr. Vincenzo Sardi advised us to collect together all the voices, both for and against. The same advice was given us by Mgr. Achille Martini, Advocate of the Saints, although he had spoken only once with the Servant of God.

We followed that advice, and the collection of judgments is kept in our Archive.

The Cardinal Protector, Rampolla, on the occasion of the introduction of the Ordinary Process, showed himself altogether favorable, and, I being present, said to Mother Carrega: «It is rather a duty».

This fame of holiness has not faded with the years, but has grown, as appeared especially on the occasion of the first fiftieth anniversary of the foundation of the Institute. Then we received, not only from our Sisters but also from lay people and from Bishops, letters extolling the virtues of the Servant of God and expressing wishes that she soon be raised to the honor of the Altars. These letters too are kept in the Archive.

§ 460
A grace attributed to the Servant of God.

Ad 40: About September or October 1900, Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, in whom a tumor the size of an egg had appeared on the breast, came to Rome to set out her misery to Mother Carrega. Having had her examined by Professor Montechiari, he, I being present, said to Mother Carrega: «Advise the Sister to have herself operated on, because it might degenerate into cancer». Of this advice, however, Mother Amante would not hear, who said: «But what, what operation? I have confidence only in my Mother Gattorno, who freed me from other miseries of mine, and will free me from this one too».

Returned to Florence, she had from Professor Grocco, who examined her, the same advice that she had had from Montechiari; she, however, remained fixed in her confidence in the Foundress, and commended herself to her. On the night of the vigil of All Saints she dreamed of the Servant of God, who said to her: «It is nothing, it is nothing, be calm»; and touched the diseased part, and giving her a little slap said to her: «Woman of little faith»; and disappeared. Waking at once, Sr. A. Amante ran with her hand to feel the diseased part, which she found partly deflated; a few days later the tumor had disappeared completely. At present she is hale and works like a martyr.

Additamentum ipsius testis 9:

The marriage of the Servant of God was celebrated in S. Lorenzo of Genoa.

While I was at the Parrocchietta, sometimes the Servant of God, writing to me, said: «I write you briefly because my hand is swollen». Then, being in the Secretariat, I noticed and saw that several times she had swollen hands. I asked Sr. A. Carrega why; but she answered me in a veiled way, incomprehensible to me. After the death of the Servant of God, however, the one who opened my eyes was Sr. Camilla Valentini, telling me that the Servant of God had the invisible stigmata.

Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega had of the Mother an esteem as of a Saint of the Altars, such that none could surpass her.

p. 281

Questioned on the criterion followed in the induction of the Witnesses in this Process, I shall say that we did not know how to proceed, and that therefore we turned to the Postulator, who told us to present all those who had been close to the Servant of God and had known her.

Now that I understand a little better how things go, I understand well that some Witnesses inducted by us will not be able to give any contribution to the Cause. Several of those Sisters who took the oath in the first sessions are no longer in this House, but scattered here and there, and one in America, who is Sr. Immacolata Cavassa, who however would be a Witness of no importance.

In 1888, the General Chapter being finished, all the voting members were received in Audience by the Holy Father Leo, who, after speaking of various things of our Institute, apostrophized the Servant of God, saying to her: «But who inspired you?». The Servant of God I then saw all humble beside the Pontifical throne, mute and mortified.

Once the Sisters of our House at Vicolo del Piombo were received in collective audience in St. Peter's, and when they were presented to him, he exclaimed: «Ah, these are the Sisters founded by that Holy woman, who is Rosa Gattorno. Tell her that I bless her, and together with her all the Sisters».

WITNESS X
Sr. ANNA MICHELINA NEGRI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 157ª of 15 November 1915 (fol. 1380) to Sess. 174ª of 19 January 1916 (fol. 1521 bis).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Maria Antonietta Negri, born on 15 April 1867 at Naples.

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, formerly music teacher, directress of the Daughters of Mary.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she knew the Servant of God: 13 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness knew her: 49 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 49 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: Having entered Religion in 1880, the witness lived together with the Servant of God until the latter's death (1900), a total therefore of 20 years.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: This testimony too is vast, detailed, with news all at first hand, extending over the last 20 years of the Servant of God. To avoid excessive enlargement of the Summarium, the answers reported here are those most interesting from the point of view of the originality of the information, and the most useful for clarifying intricate questions. In particular there emerges the careful analysis of how the Servant of God understood and carried out the role of Superior General of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, and the consequent demonstration of how she was always balanced in fulfilling her duties as mother and as foundress. The same criterion has been used in the matter of proofs about the heroic exercise of the virtues, the demonstration of which turns out weighty and full. Bearing in mind that the witness is «de visu» also as regards the last illness, the death, the funeral and the burial of the Servant of God, the testimony acquires high probative weight in this respect, as it also does regarding the proof of the fame of holiness.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1382v., testis respondit:

§ 461
General particulars of the witness.

My name is Anna Michelina Negri, daughter of the late Enrico and Maddalena Agraz. I was born at Naples on 15 April 1867. I entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne in May 1880, at Piacenza, and was received there by our Foundress, Mother Gattorno. I put on the religious habit on 4 October of the same year 1880, and made profession on the feast of St. Anne in 1881, the practice of two years of Novitiate not yet existing in the Institute and our Constitutions not yet having been approved. I made my perpetual Vows afterward on the feast of St. Anne in 1891.

My constant office was at Piacenza always that of music teacher, and in Rome, where I came in 1887, when this house was opened, the office of Directress of the Daughters of Mary was added to me.

§ 462
Scope of acquaintance.

Ad 21: I came to know the Daughters of St. Anne at Naples, they having come to Naples to nurse an ailing uncle of mine, and the Superior often spoke to me of their Foundress, and depicted her to me as a holy woman of very penitent life. I then desired to know her, and when she came once to Naples, I went to pay her a visit. She received me with much affability and invited me to stay some days in the house of the Sisters. The Servant of God then insisting much, although I had never been away from home, and my family saw my departure, even temporary, with displeasure, I yielded to the insistence of the Servant of God and stayed with her about fifteen days. In this time she showed me every kindness, and invited me to follow her to Piacenza. Her kindnesses had so attracted me that I became very fond of her, so that afterward, when the Mother went away for some time, I was desolate and wept. I followed her therefore to Piacenza, but having arrived there I began to feel the separation from my family and from my native city, so different in its aspect and movement from the one where I then found myself.

§ 463
First superior general of the Institute.

Ad 22, Proc. fol. 1397: The Servant of God at first governed all the houses of the Institute herself, but at the first Chapter, which was held at Piacenza in 1883, she was elected Mother General by full votes, and from then on she was always reconfirmed in the following Chapters, without however taking any pleasure in it, but rather with the desire to be a subject instead, as she so many times expressed herself to us.

In all the time of her long government she not only governed the Institute very well, with word and with instructions and provisions, but above all with her example.

In the admission of Postulants she not only required all papers in order, certificates, attestations, etc., but also informed herself minutely, not only about the Postulants but also about their families, to know whether in them there had been any case of illness that might afterward influence the aspirant, whether these illnesses were physical or mental. She used to say: «Better few and good». This maxim and this system of hers she inculcated on all the Superiors in acceptances. Worthy of note is that the first Aspirants admitted were those who always gave the Institute greater edification through observance and industriousness.

§ 464
She visited her communities tirelessly.

Proc. fol. 1401: The Servant of God visited her Religious Houses very often, and it can be said that she was almost always on the move. To know better their real state, she tried to arrive unexpectedly, and was most minute in her inquiries. And this solicitude of hers in the visits she had constantly until the last months of her life. For the visits she did not even care for her health, and sometimes, having arrived at the Houses, she had to go to bed at once, because she could bear no more with her illness. When she could not go personally, at the beginning she sent Sr. Benedetta Carrega and sometimes her first Secretary, Sr. Francesca Camisa. Even when the Provincials were made, she did not excuse herself from visiting the houses of the various Provinces, and it can be said that she always made the visits herself, not relying on the visits of the Provincials.

Sr. Benedetta Carrega, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, and others told me that the Servant of God, finding herself lodged in a house at Foligno, where we had many enemies, the house was set on fire by them, and the Servant of God with the Sisters passed unharmed through the flames. It must be noted that the door had already been completely taken by the flames and they had to pass through them perforce.

Her first journey to Sicily was disastrous. Not being able, because she suffered much on sea voyages, to make the crossing from Naples to Palermo, she wished, despite the contrary advice of the Doctors, to go by Reggio di Calabria and cross the strait, where there was not yet the ferry. Both because of the long journey by land (and she suffered much by land too, and I myself was a witness of it, traveling sometimes with her) and because of the crossing of the strait, which was stormy, she suffered so much that, having finally arrived at Messina, she had to go to bed, and was ill enough to cause fears for her life. Notwithstanding this, she, some years later, made the same journey again. If it were not for the sea, she used to say, I would go even to America.

Besides informing herself personally of the running of the houses when she made the visit, she kept up to date on them also by epistolary correspondence.

§ 465
Excellent qualities of government.

In the distribution of offices she did not let herself be guided by affections or partiality, but chose for them the Sisters according to their aptitude and capacity. I, on this, never heard anyone make any reproach to the Servant of God. She was also a skilled administrator of money. She did not possess a great education, because she was educated in times when not much was usually imparted to women; but it was said that if she had had occasion to educate herself more, she would have become a prodigy through her versatile talent, because, notwithstanding the little education, she understood well about accounting and every other thing. She also supervised the administration that the Superiors kept.

She required that the Sisters be treated well, but not with the superfluous, being most fond of poverty, of which she gave an example to all. The savings of the various houses were to be sent to the Generalate House, as is still done today.

§ 466
Financial difficulties at the beginning of the foundation.

In the first times of the Institute, the older Sisters told me, the food, for lack of means, was not of the best, but at times they even came to have only polenta. The Sisters, however, did not have to suffer for this, but always worked cheerfully with the Servant of God. The surpluses of the various houses, which were and are sent to the Generalate House, served the Servant of God to maintain this and other houses of ours that had need. For it is to be noted that in the houses where our Sisters are to assist the sick in their homes they had to rely on Providence for their needs, not being able to demand or ask anything for their assistance to the sick, and therefore they could sometimes be in need, and they had help from the Mother. I have said that the houses where our Sisters were destined only to the service of the sick in their homes had no special resources, and this enters into the principal purpose of our Institute, since the Servant of God founded it principally with the aim of assisting the sick gratuitously in their homes and in hospitals.

When the Servant of God required the savings of the various houses, she made it noted that they must really be from the superfluous, and woe to those Superiors who dared to send savings beyond their means, skimping too much even on the necessary in their Communities.

§ 467
She never neglected the duties of a superior because of relatives.

Ad 24, Proc. fol. 1409v.: As far as I know, and from what I have heard said, the Servant of God, in order to assist her relatives, never at any time neglected her duties toward the Institute, to such a point that her relatives even complained, such as her son and her son-in-law, who said: «after all she must always remember that she is a mother». But the Servant of God to such remarks answered: «For my children I did as much as I could, I provided for them and settled them; let that suffice for them. The first place, for me, must always be held in my mind by the Institute».

I have already said in another session something analogous about her daughter. The son-in-law especially, and the grandchildren instigated by their father, tormented the Servant of God to have money always, and the Servant of God said: «What do you want me to give you? I have given you what I could, and what I have now is all the Institute's». They made her suffer especially in her last illness. Nevertheless she gave them what was hers. I recall in particular that when the granddaughter Maria became engaged she greatly tormented her grandmother, demanding money to secure the match that had come her way. She came to torment her even while she was eating, and the poor woman rose from table with a great headache from the pressure she received from Maria.

The Servant of God was so scrupulous in matters of money that at the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Institute, when Cardinal Verga, our Protector, presented her with the approved Constitutions, she, moved, shut herself in her room, and when she came out she presented Cardinal Verga with a sealed envelope, saying to him: «Eminence, this envelope contains a hundred thousand lire, savings of the Institute in these twenty-five years. May Your Eminence dispose of them as you think best for the Institute». And the Cardinal to her: «As you have known so well how to save for the Institute, so too you will know how to use it very well. Keep it yourself».

In her last illness, when she understood that there was nothing more to hope for her health, she had all the money she kept there taken out of a wall cupboard in her bedroom, for fear of her son-in-law Gaspare, as she herself expressed it to Sr. Benedetta Carrega.

I know that her brother Checco gave the Servant of God some little thing (for it is to be known that neither her brothers nor her son ever showed themselves interested in money with her). And also the Princess of Fitalia, and I suppose some other person, gave money to the Servant of God with the intention that she use it for herself and for her relatives; and of this money the Servant of God made use to content in part the great requests of the son-in-law and the grandchildren, that is, to make them some little gift on occasions, which certainly, however, could in no way content them.

Before finishing speaking of the relatives, I shall say that the Servant of God did not go to the house of her relatives except in case of illness, and even then she never stayed to sleep, not even at the house of her sick son, to which she had been called by the Bishop of Piacenza. On this occasion only in the last days, when the son was gravely ill, she stayed to take the food that we sent her to eat.
