§ 468
The Apostolic Visitation originated from the son-in-law's complaints.

Ad 25: I know of the Apostolic visitation that our Institute had, and I believe almost for certain, according to the voices I have heard, that it was originated by the complaints and calumnies of Count Barbiellini. He went about saying, right and left, that his mother-in-law deceived people, for example: by sending Sisters without a diploma with the diploma of other Sisters unable to go to that house through illness or other cause; that she disinherited her children, that she had used her children's dowry money for the Institute and had never returned it; that she made the Sisters suffer as regards food.

I remember that once, having accompanied the Servant of God to the station, as she was leaving to visit certain houses of hers, she met at the station Cardinal Parocchi, then Vicar of His Holiness. She moved toward him and kissed his hand. Then the Cardinal said: «You too are making a little journey». «Yes, answered the Servant of God, I am going to visit certain houses in Tuscany». Present at this conversation was also Count Gaspare Barbiellini, who waited until his mother-in-law had gone away to say afterward to the Cardinal: «Yes, yes, she has tried to give Your Eminence to understand that she is going to make visits to the houses of the Institute, and instead she is going on holiday in the Apennines». Then, the train having left, he came to tell us Sisters, with great glee, that he had got the better of the Servant of God and that he had said so and so to the Cardinal Vicar. He was reproved for it, but in vain. Sometimes, not by me, who did not dare, but by Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, these things were reported to the Servant of God, who answered: «Let him say it; if he says that I am wicked, he is in the right, because I have never been good. As for the particular accusations, however, I know that I am not guilty».

Barbiellini boasted of knowing Serafini, the Apostolic Administrator, very well, and of being his friend, of having been at school with him; and when he learned that he would come as Apostolic Visitor to visit our houses, he often went to visit him and to slander the Servant of God, as he himself afterward told me. He said she was a pretender, a liar, and always for money. He possessed a great art of coloring the falsest things as true, and asserted that he had proofs in hand, that he possessed documents, etc., etc. It was no use my making remarks to the contrary; he asserted that if he said so it must be quite true, that I was a child and knew nothing. To the assertion I made to him, when he said that the Sisters here and there suffered as regards food, that he was an outsider and therefore could know nothing, that here in this house nothing was lacking to us, and that in the houses where I had gone with the Servant of God I had heard no complaints and had seen nothing deficient in food or otherwise, he gave the same answer I have said, that I was a child, that I did not understand things, and that these really were as he said. And he told me that he had said these things also to the Apostolic Administrator, Monsignor Serafini. Of the relations between Count Barbiellini and the Servant of God, I now recall that he took advantage of our using this or that shopkeeper to send for articles for himself too on our account. But the Servant of God held firm, and inexorably made him pay the bill due from him. I recall that once, as music teacher needing strings for the harp, I presented myself to the Servant of God to have permission to go and buy them. The Servant of God gave me a good exhortation on poverty, telling me that I must economize on the price as much as I could, although Providence assisted us more than necessary. I answered the Mother that I really sought economy, that I spliced the broken strings, and that I tried in every way also not to have the trouble of coming to ask her for such permissions. I had the permission asked and bought the strings at the Ceccherini shop in Via Nazionale. In those days Maria, Barbiellini's daughter, also needed strings, and her father also went to Ceccherini to buy them in our name, and the bill was sent to the Servant of God. Having received this second bill, the Servant of God called me to reproach me for so much waste of strings. And I, answering her that I knew nothing of this second bill, with the Superior's permission went at once to Ceccherini, from whom I learned that the second expense had been made in our name by Count Barbiellini. I at once warned him to hand over nothing to anyone without a note from us; and the matter being reported to the Mother, she did not pay, and wished the Count to settle his own bill.

§ 469
The Servant of God serenely accepted the Apostolic Visitation.

The Servant of God naturally felt displeasure at the Apostolic Visitation, but she did not complain, and received it serenely, saying: «God has willed it, His will be done; it will be for the good of the Institute». She never suggested to us how we should conduct ourselves in the answers to the Visitor; on the contrary she exhorted us to tell the whole truth, and never even tried to know what the Visitor had asked us, or what we had answered, although we were not under oath of secrecy about what he asked or we answered.

The impression I received from my interrogation and from that of some other Sisters is that the accusations which had provoked the visitation turned especially on the treatment as regards food and clothing. The Servant of God was always respectful toward the Visitor, who, as far as I know, remained well satisfied with our answers. The Servant of God told us afterward one day: «I tell you for your consolation that the Visitor remained very pleased with the visit made to you, because he found all the Sisters thinking in the same way and very concordant in their answers, and that he had acquired much esteem for the Institute».

Ad 27, Proc. fol. 1422: The Servant of God always practiced the Theological virtues, Faith, Hope and Charity, and the Cardinal ones, Prudence, Justice, Fortitude and Temperance, and the connected ones, Humility, Chastity, Poverty and Obedience.

§ 470
Heroic practice of faith.

And as regards the virtue of Faith, the Servant of God not only believed firmly, but I myself heard her exclaim: «Oh, if only I were given the occasion to shed my blood for the Faith!», and she exhorted Sisters and Novices to have the same sentiments. In the things of our Faith she was extremely well instructed, and when she went to the Novitiate to give conferences, we too went, and it seemed to us that we were hearing a Preacher.

Her conferences dealt either with some point of the Rule or with the Catechism. She also questioned them to see whether they had understood, and we were instructed on our duties and on the Catechism, showing that her great concern was that her Sisters be instructed in the Catechism in order to be able to instruct others. She wanted the local Superiors of the other Houses also to give similar conferences to their Sisters, and she herself gave them when she went on visitation.

At the beginning of the foundation, in our house at Piacenza there were little girls, and the Servant of God occupied herself personally with instructing them in the Catechism.

In this Church of Via Merulana she wished the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary to be instituted; and although she did not occupy herself personally with them, she wanted to see them from time to time to say some good word to them, and recommended to the Sisters in charge their Religious instruction. The old Daughters of Mary still remember the great affection that our Mother showed them, and always mention her.

In the holy year she wished our Association of the Daughters of Mary to make the visits too to gain the Holy Jubilee. We made the first visit on 29 April, seven days before her death, together with other Unions of Daughters of Mary. The Servant of God then called me, who had accompanied the Daughters of Mary, so that I might tell her how the visits had gone, and exclaimed: «Oh, if Our Lady grants me the grace of recovering a little, I too would come to make visits with the Daughters of Mary». She wanted catechetical prizes to be given so that the girls would attend. She also wanted the Daughters of Mary to take part in the singing in our Church, and when they had sung well she rejoiced with them and sent them sweets, sugared almonds, etc. She also instituted the Congregation of the Luigini in our Church, which afterward ceased when we lacked the Priest who took care of them.

We have several Sisters who were formerly Daughters of Mary, and all have turned out excellently. She also inculcated on the other Superiors that they found and cultivate the pious unions of the Daughters of Mary, because she used to say that great fruit is drawn from these pious associations.

§ 471
Apostolic ardor born of faith.

She burned with desire for the conversion of unbelievers and of sinners, and would have been ready, as she said, to give her blood for them. «Blessed is she, she told us, who can convert a sinner, because she has made sure of the salvation of her own soul».

She prayed and exhorted us all to pray, also in our private prayers, for the conversion of unbelievers and sinners. She desired that her Institute be called to some mission among unbelievers, as then happened. When some group was then to leave for the said Missions, she encouraged them with such accents that the Sisters felt afterward their spirit full of sweetness and courage.

§ 472
An uncommon spirit of prayer.

Proc. fol. 1430: The Servant of God possessed the spirit of prayer in an eminent degree, and inspired it in us too. She never wasted time: she either worked or prayed. She prayed in all the time left free to her, and at night too, being unable to rest because of her ailments, she prayed. We Sisters know it, because when she was worse, one of us staying to watch over her, we saw that she was praying. And even when she was not afflicted by her illness, she sometimes said, with indifference and in a way that evidently showed she did not speak out of vanity: «Last night I could not sleep, and so I said fifteen decades of the Rosary; a hundred Requiem aeternam, etc.».

It was well seen that the Servant of God, when she prayed, stood in the presence of God. Especially after Communion, in which she spent no less than an hour of thanksgiving kneeling on the floor, she was seen so absorbed and motionless that she seemed not even to feel it if one went to shake or question her; it seemed she did not hear. Sometimes we charged Sr. Benedetta Carrega, Secretary, to go and ask her something after Communion, and she would answer us: «It is useless, she does not hear».

In Church she did not concern herself with who came in or went out: she was always kneeling on the floor, unless she was very ill; then she sat for a few minutes and then knelt again. Not only did she stay motionless and not wander with her eyes here and there in the Church, but she did not want even us to turn our heads. It was seen that the Servant of God was always in the presence of the Lord, as appeared from her words, her aspect, her bearing, not only to us Sisters but also to outside persons who had occasion to speak with her, whom I often heard say: «But your Mother is a Saint».

§ 473
Devotion to the Passion of the Lord. Penances.

Proc. fol. 1440: The point of the Passion of Our Lord preferred by the Servant of God for meditation was, as she told us, Jesus Crucified.

She had in her secret room at Piacenza a Christ about twenty-five centimeters tall, which, as I heard from other sisters (among them Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega and Sr. Anna Nazzarena Pastorini, both deceased), had detached itself from the cross several times, although they had fixed it there so many times. This Christ is now kept in a case made by the Princess of Fitalia.

Another Crucifix, about seven or eight centimeters tall, was taken from her on the very day she took to her bed for the last time, by Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia, from her Breast, where she herself had placed it. Sr. Serafina told me this. Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega then narrated to me that the Servant of God had made herself a cut on the left side of the Breast and had introduced a small Crucifix into it.

In her secret room at Piacenza a very large Cross was found formed of two tree trunks. In the arms of the cross and at the foot there were iron devices made so as to be able to clamp the wrists and feet of whoever placed himself on it in the form of a cross.

There was found also in that same room, again after her death, another cross formed with two benches, which made one suppose that the Servant of God lay upon it to rest.

That room at Piacenza I have called secret because during her life no living soul could ever enter it. And when she was ill and therefore needed assistance, so as not to let anyone enter that room, she preferred to stay in some other, for example in that of Sr. Benedetta Carrega.

In that room, after her death, it was found that the bed was formed of two boards with a straw mattress on top. In the pillow was found a crown formed of thorny things. There were found also a discipline formed with iron points, other little chains also with iron points, and a sort of cuirass formed of bristly things, and irons and pins. The windows of that room had no panes, or rather the panes existed at one time, but the Servant of God, so as not to let anyone in, when they broke replaced them with paper. The washstand found there was of ordinary old wood, as ordinary and old were the basin and the jug and the two or three chairs. The furnishing was completed by a rough small lamp, an image of St. Anne on the bed, and an old screen before the door to prevent any indiscreet glance when she opened the door.

§ 474
Trust in God and resignation.

Proc. fol. 1459: Who can doubt that the Servant of God had and exercised also the virtue of Hope? She expected nothing from this world, and all her hope was placed in God. «Even with us Religious, — she told us —, the devil tries to draw some profit, soliciting our heart to attach itself to the things of this earth, but remember that all is vanity and affliction of spirit, and that we can expect everything only from God».

In all difficulties she was resigned to the will of God, to whom she turned in prayer: «May the will of God be done»; this was her habitual motto in sorrows and difficulties; and when something went wrong for us, she exhorted us to abandon ourselves to the will of God. And if we complained of not having been heard after many prayers, she told us: «It is a sign that it is not good for your soul that this thing go according to your designs». She had no attachment to her ideas and to her will, but showed herself very submissive and deferential in everything to Superiors.

Notwithstanding, however, her unlimited trust in God, she made use of human means, and in difficulties did not strive to escape them, but abandoned herself in God. Her trust in the Providence of God was rewarded by the Lord even in a prodigious way. «Abandon yourselves to the Providence of God, she told us, and you will never lack anything». And this abandonment she suggested also to outside persons, whether desolate or poor or afflicted in any way.

§ 475
Most ardent love of God.

As regards Charity toward God, not only did she try to avoid even the slightest offense to the Lord, but she also sought that every other soul avoid it: «Blessed is that soul, she told us, who in the evening can say: today I have committed no deliberate fault». And she said it with such an accent that we well understood that she could say it of herself every evening. So great, moreover, was her presence and mastery of herself that surely nothing offensive to the Lord could escape her. She spoke to us much of the general and particular examination to keep us far from fault. When she heard of the wickedness committed in the world, I noticed that she felt great pain, and was even transformed in her face, and she exhorted us to make some act of reparation with ejaculatory prayers, with little spiritual flowers, with mortifications for the sins committed in the world. The last three days of carnival she wanted the exposition of the Blessed Sacrament in our Chapel in reparation for the sins committed on those days.

When she went on visitation to our houses that have charge of some Hospital, she went through the wards, and to each sick person suggested either resignation in suffering or care to avoid sin. When she then met some sick person indifferent to receiving the Sacraments, or averse, according to the case she set herself with all her might to overcome the indifference or the aversion; and if she had been forced to leave at once, great were the recommendations she made of the sick person to her Sisters, and I know of no case in which she did not succeed. «I had the consolation, — she told us —, that of all the sick who passed through my hands, with God's help, none died without the Sacraments».

Proc. fol. 1468: Charity toward neighbor: She tried to insinuate into every soul she approached the spirit of prayer.

§ 476
Spirit of prayer and apostolate.

Her mother Adelaide told us that the Servant of God, when she was still in the world, occupied herself with the Daughters of Mary and inculcated in them the spirit of prayer. This too she wanted the Sisters to do for the Daughters of Mary, for the schoolgirls, and for the sick. «Teach them, — she said —, to pray more with the heart than with words», noting that the essence of prayer lies in the elevation of our mind and our heart to God. Hence we Sisters especially, she further told us, can be in continual prayer, even in the midst of our tasks. In the Novitiate she ordered that there be many prayers also during work; and to us Sisters she advised saying the Rosary when we were gathered together in some room working. «Thus, — she said —, you will be more united with God, and will avoid breaking silence; you will not waste time and will have the advantage of common prayer».

§ 477
Solicitous for the spiritual salvation of neighbor.

When the Servant of God prayed, she seemed almost alienated from the senses, as I have already said speaking of the thanksgiving after Communion, and I myself noticed her transformation in the face, the burning eyes, and not only then but also in her room and when she was ill.

From what I have said one can well deduce that the Servant of God was most solicitous for the spiritual salvation of neighbor, but her care extended also to his temporal good. I never heard that the Servant of God ever spoke ill of anyone, and she always tried to cover with the mantle of charity even the least faults.

I know that in general she had enemies, but she always kept her charitable spirit toward them, and sometimes when she was told that such a person, by such an action, had well deserved ill of her, «Oh, I have well deserved this and more» she would answer. And she added all the excuses with holy ingenuity, blaming herself.

If we had some small resentment against someone, she demanded that we forgive at once, and if some small clash had occurred among us Sisters, she wanted us, before going to bed, to have asked each other's pardon; otherwise she would not have permitted us Communion on the following day.

§ 478
Charity toward the poor.

Proc. fol. 1475: Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega tried to keep her things apart, and hidden, because the Servant of God would have taken the opportunity to deprive herself of them in favor of the poor. She often sent soups and broth too to the poor sick who were without help, and many times she carried them herself. She exhorted us too to much charity toward the poor, and especially the sick, and we tried to deprive ourselves of this or that thing and brought it to her, knowing that we gave her great pleasure, as indeed she showed us, because thus she had greater means of satisfying charity toward the poor.

She wanted us Sisters to be wholly for the good of neighbor in every respect, and she spoke of it to us, to the Superiors when they left for some house, and when she visited the houses, and to the Novices. She wanted charity to be practiced also among ourselves, helping one another even at the cost of some sacrifice, so that when we were ill one would lend herself for the other; and to the sick she inculcated charity toward the Sister nurses.

§ 479
Prudence and discretion.

The Servant of God was most prudent. She fled idleness and was never in it for a minute. When in recreation with us, she always kept some work in her hands, always made conversation on useful things, and even from a joke drew her moral aim.

In the last year the Servant of God suffered much from drowsiness, but did not give in, and always worked. When we noticed her tiredness, and saw her bow her head, we begged her to withdraw a little to her room, but she answered us: «No, no! let us not yield to idleness».

Before the last year she stayed up even at night to attend personally as much as she could to the correspondence; to the most distant ones, moreover, she never for any reason ceased to reply personally.

When she had to open some new house, and for other grave affairs of the Institute, she had recourse not only to prayer, which in her was habitual, but also to the Cardinal Protector. Before taking a decision she reflected, «for, — as she told us —, one must not precipitate decisions, but must take counsel above all with God and then with Superiors». Sometimes I heard her say: «Pray much to the Lord, because I have an important affair». For similar cases she called the Mistress of Novices, saying to her: «Have your Novices pray, because I have a somewhat important affair». And she sometimes had the Blessed Sacrament exposed also for such affairs.

The Princess of Fitalia told us that she did nothing without having taken counsel of the Servant of God, either by word of mouth or by letter. I also know in general that other persons too turned to her for counsel, but I could not specify them.

In the government of the Institute and in its administration, for my part, I always found her most prudent. She studied the characters of the Sisters and knew how to take them on their own side.

She recommended to the Superiors also that they study characters themselves, and warned them that, while one could be taken with rigor, the other had to be taken with gentleness. «See, — she said to them —, in a ward there may be many sick, but the same medicines do not suit all equally: one must know how to adapt them».

There was no Sister corrected by her who left her room offended, so well did she know how to make corrections.

§ 480
She was very mortified in everything.

Most temperate was the Servant of God in everything, indeed mortified. She never drank wine, and only in the last years was she induced to drink watered wine (more water than wine) out of obedience to the Cardinal Protector and the Doctor; and then «behold, — she told us —, see, I had to reach old age to become a drunkard». In the morning she took a small cup of black coffee without sugar, without bread, and never added milk, as she never took it at any other time. She always ate meatless, and this too she wanted to be ordinary. Seeing her suffering, sometimes Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega had some decent fish procured for her, but she scolded her and said to her: «You know I do not like it», and ended by giving the fish to this one or that, and sometimes I too gained, she knowing that I liked it, and she remained with nothing. If the cook made a mistake in cooking or seasoning so that the dish turned out little pleasing, then the Servant of God ate it more willingly, so that among us the saying had arisen, when we saw the Servant of God finishing the dish: «It is clear that today the dish was bad, because the Mother finished it».

p. 297

Proc. fol. 1485: On some solemnities it is the custom to serve at table some extra dish for us, but her food was constantly that, and so it was the despair of Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, who would have wished that at least at Christmas and on some other solemnity she eat a little choice fish, but the Servant of God held fast to her salt cod and stockfish, potatoes, broccoli, etc., saying: «Let my gluttony be satisfied». She never drank between meals. Sometimes when we felt great burning heat in summer, we asked her too whether she felt hot and parched; and if she answered yes, we saw to it that she took some drink, but she answered us: «Leave it: drinking outside meals does me harm».

On St. Anne's day there is the custom of serving ice cream after dinner to the Community. So too on St. Rose's. And she delighted in distributing it to us, but for herself she alleged the reason that, being in a sweat, it would do her harm.

She always mended her own things herself, when she saw there was need; and she did not mind much whether the cloth was more faded or not than the habit, so that we often laughed and said to her: «Oh, is it Carnival, Mother?», and she laughed with us and told us: «I like old clothes so much, because they fit the person better, while new ones make me feel encumbered». Her bed was made of a straw mattress and a woolen blanket; no sheets or anything else. And this until her death. A black shawl served as a sheet, which she took with her even when traveling.

In illness she did not want costly medicines, saying: «I am old-fashioned; in modern medicines I have not much confidence». When she had some cold, we, returning home, brought her some fine lozenge; she, thanking us for the attention, did not use them, but distributed them to others, and especially to the nurse, charging her to carry them to those who needed them.

§ 481
Firm in decisions taken; love of chastity.

The Servant of God possessed the virtue of fortitude, and there were no prayers that availed to move her from a decision she believed just.

More than once it happened that a Sister asked, or was requested by administrations of Hospitals or schools, to remain in this or that house, adducing the good that would be lacking through her absence, but the Servant of God, if she had believed that her change was for the good of that house or of that Sister, there was no chance of her yielding, whatever means or reasons were used, even under the threat of seeing that house closed. She was yielding and deferential, as I have already said, to the counsels of the higher Superiors and of her Assistants.

From what I have already said one can well gather how the Servant of God guarded the virtue of Chastity, not only for herself but also for her Sisters. I do not know the names, but I know that some Sister was rebuked and punished by her for some levity. Her reserve was such that even in her last illness she never let herself be helped to dress, and did not even permit the doctors to touch her even over the bedclothes, however much the doctors and Sisters insisted.

Of poverty and obedience I have already spoken enough to deduce how she possessed and exercised them. In her last illness she submitted entirely to the doctors, except in being touched, and, poor woman, she was induced also to let an enema be given her, with great sacrifice.

In some illness, when some costly medicine was prescribed, she begged the doctor to substitute some other of lower price; but if the doctor appealed to obedience, she yielded. The doctor Montechiari, however, who knew her well, tried to content her. The costly medicines refused by her were only those where explicit obedience to the doctor was not involved.

She wanted the Sisters to obey to the letter, and admitted no reply.

§ 482
She excelled in the practice of humility.

Proc. fol. 1493: The Servant of God possessed and exercised the virtue of humility: she never wished to be called General or Foundress. «I did not found the Institute, — she said —, but St. Anne did. I was only an instrument in the hands of God. You think I am goodness knows what, but it is because you do not know me enough». She never spoke of her own things and much less exalted them. And if in someone her ability shone, she tried to cover it, and give the credit to another. For example, if to the foundation of some house she sent either Sr. Benedetta Carrega or Sr. Vincenza, her first Secretary, and praises came to her for the well-succeeded foundation, she turned them back upon her envoys, reserving nothing for herself.

She did not even permit us to kiss her hands. Going to visit Cardinals, she announced herself only with the name of Sr. Rosa Gattorno, as Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega told me, and sat in the anteroom, not in evidence, and so many who had come after passed ahead of her, and she waited patiently.

Not many days ago Miss Adele Pelli, who from the time of Mother Gattorno belonged to our Congregation of the Daughters of Mary, told me that she would never forget the act of humility that the Servant of God once performed with her. The Daughters of Mary having presented themselves to the Servant of God for good wishes, I do not remember on what occasion, Pelli being left without a chair, because the others were occupied by the Daughters of Mary, the Servant of God offered her her own.

I recall that once the Servant of God had to point out to the Superiors gathered together for the Spiritual exercises the defects she had noticed on her round of their houses; after setting them out with very mild words and with much gentleness, she knelt before them asking pardon if she had exceeded in speaking. The Superiors were greatly moved by that act, left the meeting hall with tears in their eyes, and so, when we asked those Sisters what had happened, they narrated to us what I have said.

At Piacenza I myself saw her so many times wash the dishes and help in other tasks in the kitchen. I saw her also sweep other rooms besides her own. And when she did these services, quite content she told us: «These things, you see, I know how to do very well, these suit me, while you think I am goodness knows what». In this house I heard it told that a Novice of this same house was surprised one day by the Servant of God while sweeping the corridor of this guesthouse; she took the broom from her hand saying: «Let me do it, for I am cold, and so I warm myself a little», and she went on sweeping.

§ 483
She reached a degree above the common in the practice of the virtues.

Ad 28: And she perfected herself so much as to reach in the said virtues not only a degree above the common, but I can without doubt say that she reached the heroic degree, that is, of a Saint of the altars, that is, in a most perfect degree, with promptness, ease, spontaneity, as if it had been a second nature. And from what the Mother of the Servant of God, Adelaide, used to tell, it seems that she exercised them in heroic degree even from girlhood.

Ad 33, Proc. fol. 1503: The Servant of God died on 6 May 1900 at a quarter past nine in the morning.

p. 300

§ 484
Last illness and holy death.

She had been ill all winter and had already returned ill from Sampierdarena in September 1899, and those who accompanied her wished the doctor to accompany her as well, because they feared she might die on the road. Arrived in Rome, we saw her so worn that it caused us such compassion that we did not even dare to approach her. She stayed at first some days in bed, but then, by her great strength of spirit, she got up, but was always very suffering, so that Professor Montechiari, her attending physician, said: «I do not know how the Mother can resist, and how she can resist and apply herself to the affairs of the Institute, write letters, etc.».

In November, the episcopal consecration of the Most Eminent Granito di Belmonte having taken place in our Church, I recall that the Servant of God dragged herself about the house, observing and giving orders so that everything might proceed in the most perfect manner. In consequence, however, of the strain of those days she was forced to keep to bed for a little while longer. She then rose again and, until the end, it was a continual alternation between going to bed and getting up, and going to her study, because as soon as she felt a little strength she at once put it to profit for work. So it lasted until the last week, indeed until the last days, in which she was struck by the peritonitis of which she then died.

Professor Montechiari had told us some time before that the Mother had only a few months of life left, but we did not believe him, it seeming impossible to us that the Lord would take our Mother from us, and also because we always saw her full of courage. On Holy Thursday she wished to be accompanied to the Choir loft to visit the Sepulchre. I recall that on that occasion she was seized by a faintness, from which, having recovered, she knelt and stayed long in prayer with such devotion that she seemed rapt out of her senses. I was present.

She died on a Sunday.

§ 485
Attitude of the relatives at the death of the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 1512v.: At the moment when the Servant of God expired there were present Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, Sr. Anna Amante La Barbera, Sr. Camilla Valentini, Sr. Anna Consolata Massinelli, then Provincial of Northern Italy and now ill at Ovada, Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia, Fr. Agostino Donadio, and Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri. I had gone out of the room at that moment. The relatives, among them the two brothers Francesco and Federico, were in the house, but at that moment were not in the room of the Servant of God, having stayed here all night. The brothers behaved very well toward the Servant of God, having always been good and affectionate; not so the son-in-law, who thought of nothing but money. Already during the night Count Gaspare, in the room adjoining the Chapel, had asked me where the Servant of God kept the valuables, to which I answered that I knew nothing. But he added: «you have charge of the things of the Chapel, chalices, silver ciboria, etc. See whether there might be a way to pinch something; after all, who would know anything». And I: «You want to send me to hell too; go there by yourself, if you wish». Then the same Count Gaspare said to his daughter Maria: «You who had more access to grandmother will know where she kept her keys; and then as soon as she dies, open the drawers a little, and look for where she keeps her things». And Maria agreed. But I did not want to hear more, and then, nauseated, I left.

It is to be observed here that when the Servant of God died there was nothing left in the cupboards, because she, before dying, had already handed everything over to Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega. And so Maria did not even manage to find the keys.

Ad 34: The Servant of God being dead, the brothers presented us their condolences and went away. The son-in-law and the others of the family withdrew too, but returned shortly after, the Notary Monti being present, and had the drawers and the wardrobe opened, but finding nothing, the granddaughter Maria flew into a rage and began to scream, so that we had to close the windows and the door so that it might not be heard outside. She told the Sisters that they were thieves.

At noon on Monday, as I said, she was carried to our private Chapel, where she stayed all night and the next day she was carried to the Church, where the funeral was celebrated in the presence of many people and many Sisters, among them fifty come from elsewhere. The gas that developed from the body, when it was closed and sealed in the zinc coffin, was so much that, the coffin itself having swollen, it could no longer fit in the walnut one; and therefore a little hole had to be made in the zinc one, and so the gas came out with such force that it gave a whistle, and then the lid of the zinc coffin sank, and thus it could fit in the walnut one.

It having been discussed who should hold the cords of the hearse in the funeral procession, Count Barbiellini maintained that this honor must belong to those of the family; but against him the Mother's brother, Federico, observed that the Mother had by now left the family for her Sisters, and that therefore this honor belonged to them. For this the Count Barbiellini did not even attend the funeral, and went so far as to make this gesture: at the moment the hearse was moving in the middle of the street he passed ostentatiously in front of it, without even raising his hat. As to the right of holding the cord and this last gesture of Count Barbiellini, I learned it from Mother Anna Benedetta Carrega.

The hearse was of the first class. When the coffin was carried to the hearse, the crowd and the press to see it were so great that it took no little effort to make way. I do not remember all the names of those who held the cords: among them, however, I recall Mother Carrega, Mother Speranza, Sr. Anna Borromea, and Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia.

The Daughters of Mary were at the head of the procession, and I must note that they came very willingly, and their relatives came too. Many people accompanied her to the city gate, and many still to the Cemetery. Among these there were also many distinguished persons with their carriages.

Ad 35: At that time we did not yet have our tomb in the Cemetery, and the body of the Servant of God was placed in the square on the right, just as one enters the Cemetery. After a year it was removed from that place and placed in our present tomb, precisely above the entrance door of the Chapel. The inscription is always the same that was affixed at the beginning.

§ 487
Fame of holiness. Visits to the tomb.

Ad 36: In the funeral procession I heard many persons say that a Saint had died, and this I heard said also when her body was in the Church during the funeral, etc.

Ad 37: We Sisters, and I with them, go from time to time to visit the tomb of our Mother; the Princess of Fitalia, I know, when she comes to Rome never fails to go and visit the tomb of the Servant of God, and this she does out of the veneration she has for the Servant of God herself, whom she truly esteems a Saint.

Ad 38: The Servant of God enjoyed a true fame of holiness in life for her virtues proper to a saint of the altars, and also for her supernatural and extraordinary gifts. With as many persons as I spoke during her life, all spoke to me of our Mother as of a saint of the altars; whether these persons were Sisters, or lay people, or Priests, but I always mean to speak of serious persons. And this fame did not cease with her life, but rather I would say has increased after her death. Among the persons who have esteemed and esteem her a saint of the altars, I can cite not only the Princess of Fitalia, but also Mrs. Maria Fausti, the Marchioness Emilia Carrega, her sister-in-law Edvige Carrega, the Princess Belmonte of Palermo and her daughters, the mother of Cardinal Belmonte, now deceased, the sisters of the same Cardinal, his brother, the Priest Professor Amirante, a witness inducted in the Process of Naples, Canon Bonini of Piacenza, Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri, Fr. Bernardino da Porto Gruaro, General of the Minors, who many times confessed the Servant of God, Mgr. Costa of Piacenza, Fr. Agostino Donadio of the Minims (the last three deceased) and many others. And I hold that this fame of holiness is most just and due, and certainly there was no artifice of any sort on anyone's part to awaken, sustain, and increase it.

Ad 39, Proc. fol. 1521v.: I know of no one, apart from the family of the Servant of God's son-in-law, except her daughter, by whom anything has been written or said against the fame of holiness of the Servant of God and of her virtues.

I know that Count Barbiellini, among the accusations of which I have already spoken against the Servant of God, brought also this one, that she made use of the diplomas of some Sisters to have other Sisters teach school, but I never knew anything of this; and the Sisters to whom Barbiellini presented such an accusation also replied that they knew nothing of it, and that it was not true.

Et expleto examine super Interrogatoriis, rogata fuit R. Testis super Articulis, super quibus (Proc. fol. 1513 bis), respondit:

I have read the articles of the Postulator up to Article 16, p. 60. I do not know all the things reported there; but on the whole they correspond to the idea I have of the Servant of God, and it did not seem to me that they are exaggerated. Reading them, some things came to my mind which I too knew, but which I had forgotten in my deposition.

§ 488
Clarifications on the foundation at Piacenza.

I too have heard of her first journey to Rome, which she made with a friend of hers, whose name I do not know, and how she met D. Cogrossi, on leaving Rome; that she stopped at Piacenza, where Cogrossi proposed two spiritual directors to her. I too had heard it told in the Institute that, in the audience she had from Pius IX, the Servant of God set before him the difficulties for the foundation of an Institute, very grave for her, who was a mother of a family, having children and parents still needing her assistance; and that the Holy Father said to her: «Take care, Rosa, that you must do the will of God, if you do not wish to meet his punishments; and this is his will». And that she left the Pope's audience all animated and comforted.

I also heard it said that it was the two directors presented by Cogrossi who advised her to found her institution at Piacenza, and that she acceded to their advice, and that she then went to Genoa, where she found other obstacles also on the part of the Archbishop, who made use of her in so many pious works that were going very well through her wise and prudent work; that she then turned to her Crucifix, to which she prayed much; and that she then returned to the Archbishop, whom she found all changed, and who said to her: «Go then, where the Lord calls you», that the Servant of God then made all the preparations to go to Piacenza without disclosing her plan to her parents, and that she disclosed it only two hours before her departure; and that it was then that the old father broke into sobs and that her mother lay down on the threshold to prevent her daughter from going out.

I recall that I too heard it told that the aforesaid two Directors suggested to the Servant of God to make a first rule for her foundation and that, she refusing through her supposed incapacity, they entrusted this task to a certain Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, of the Gentlemen of the Mission of St. Vincent de Paul, who was a somewhat strange Saint; that he set to work and composed the constitutions in the form of a dialogue between St. Anne, Mother Gattorno, and a religious, and that these constitutions were not approved by the Holy See.

I also remembered, reading the Articles, having heard from the Sisters, and always principally from Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, her Secretary, and from her other Assistants, that in another audience the Pope (to whom she had set out the difficulties found with the Holy Congregation over the constitutions presented) imposed on her to write them herself, and that she obeyed. I also recall that in the second audience the Pope granted her, having asked her what name she had given to her Institute, and she having answered that she called them Daughters of Mary Immaculate, the Pope added: «For now let it be so, until by divine inspiration you know the true name that you must give the Institute». Furthermore, I too heard it said that, as the Servant of God was praying in the first little Chapel at Piacenza, the Blessed Virgin Immaculate appeared to her, saying: «The name you will give to your Institute will be that of Daughters of St. Anne, my Mother». And likewise in the reading of the Articles it came back to me that the Servant of God, praying in the said Chapel for the precise form to give the habit of her Sisters, St. Anne appeared to her dressed as we are, and presenting her with the veil and the coif said: «Behold how you shall clothe your daughters».

§ 489
General particulars of the witness and scope of acquaintance.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1528v., testis respondit:

My name is Tommaso Monti, son of the late Angelo and Caterina Buti. I was born in Rome on 3 December 1831. I am a Government Notary and emeritus Chancellor of the Vicariate of Rome.

Ad 7: I came to know the Servant of God in 1873, I think, through Fr. Agostino Donadio of the Minims, for a notarial act that I was invited to make, and from then on I very often had occasion to approach her by reason of my profession. The Servant of God was a woman little expansive, and with me reserved, and outside business it was difficult for her to enter into other subjects with me.

The knowledge of the things I shall say is not founded on the Articles of the Postulator, which I have not even read, nor on his obituary notes, but only on what I have seen and what I have heard from trustworthy persons.

§ 490
Relations of the Servant of God with her family.

I know that the Servant of God was born in Genoa, of a well-off family, and that she married and, very young, was left a widow with two children, and by a kind of inspiration founded the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, having as cooperator Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega.

The Servant of God was much afflicted, especially by her son-in-law, for motives of money and because of his excessive claims. The son-in-law, moreover, did not leave his mother-in-law's Institute in peace even after her death, and it came to a long lawsuit, which was settled by compromise only a few years ago.

I know that the brothers of the Servant of God lent their assistance for the building of the House and Church of the Daughters of St. Anne in Via Merulana, and that when the time came to settle accounts between them, there was much to endure because of the claims, remarks and conditions of Mr. Federico. The Servant of God also desired that next to the said House another be built for the dwelling of her married daughter, as it seems to me the Sisters also said, and in this building Mr. Federico lent himself much, while the other brother, as it seems to me, wanted none of it.

Speaking sometimes with the Sisters, especially with Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega, they told me that they believed their Foundress did penances, that she even wore the hair shirt, and that she was a woman of virtue.

The Servant of God told me, as it seems certain to me, that, finding herself in Naples in a certain period, she could not go out of the house without donations, offerings, etc. being made to her, and this seems to me to have been a proof that that Institute had arisen according to the will of God. In the said conversation that the Servant of God held with me, I could not notice, nor can I now think, that there was the slightest sense of vanity, and I always noticed her rather as humble, most humble, and a woman of virtue, as she revealed herself to me by her bearing and in the handling of business.

In the act of settlement made with her brother Federico and in any other act drawn up by me, I always noticed in her a sense of justice, and that she did not let herself be overcome by fraternal and maternal love or by anything else to the detriment of her Institute.

When the Servant of God thought of making her holographic will, I had some talks alone with her, and on that occasion she told me that all she could give of her own to her daughter she had given, that it seemed to her she had placed her well financially, that she believed she could no longer claim anything from her, and that all she then possessed was the Institute's property.

I was not present when the Servant of God died, but I arrived shortly after, called by the Sisters. I found in the Sisters' Convent Fr. Agius, Secretary of the Apostolic Visitor of the Institute, Count Barbiellini, son-in-law of the Servant of God, and I do not remember well whether a daughter of his. A small inventory was made of the things that were in the room of the Servant of God, and when we had finished it, I noticed that Barbiellini, insalutato hospite, had gone away. I do not remember that incidents arose on that occasion.

I recall that the Sisters told me that once, her brother Federico having fallen gravely ill, she ran at once to his bedside and, to the attendants who wanted to prevent any religious person from entering near the sick man, she said resolutely that, being a sister, she wished to enter, and she entered. On that occasion, however, Federico did not die.

§ 491
A woman of uncommon virtue.

I always esteemed the Servant of God, after having dealt with her at length, as a woman of uncommon virtue, as I deduced from the facts of the growth of her Institute and from her bearing in handling business. I would not even exclude that she be worthy of the honor of the altars, but I have no particular facts to allege in support of this impression of mine; and I also have the impression that one day she may be on the Altars, because for the long time I approached her I always knew her as a woman of superior virtue.

I also heard others speak of her, but the conversation on her virtues was not gone into deeply.

I never heard anyone speak ill of the Servant of God.

§ 492
General particulars of the witness and scope of acquaintance.

My name is Anna Evangelista (in the world Maddalena) Piscopo, daughter of the late Stefano and of Marianna Piscopo. I was born at Melito, Province of Naples, on 2 April 1872, I think.

§ 494
Relations between the daughter houses and the generalate house.
§ 495
She recommended supporting the Sisters well.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1566v., testis respondit:

§ 496
General particulars of the witness and scope of acquaintance.

My name is Ancilla Briccoli (in the world Marianna), daughter of the late Bartolomeo and Maria Visani.

I was born at Brisighella, Province of Ravenna; I do not remember precisely the year: I know, however, that I am not yet 60. I entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne in 1879 at Piacenza. I was received by the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno herself, and put on the habit on 31 December of the same year 1879. In the following year, for the feast of St. Anne, I made my first vows. I left the Novitiate ten days after I had put on the habit and went to Borgo S. Donnino, where I stayed about two and a half months.

Ad 17, Proc. fol. 1595: I heard from the Sisters that before founding the Institute the Servant of God had occupied herself much with the Daughters of Mary with much zeal; and that the Archbishop had entrusted to her the task of revising the rules of that Association. In our Houses it was always sought, and is sought, that the Association of the Daughters of Mary be founded in them, because it was always said that it was a thing very dear and desired by the Servant of God.

From the Sisters I learned that the rules of our Institute are the work of the Servant of God and of her prayers.

§ 497
Prudence in the government of the Institute.

Ad 22: The Servant of God was the first Superior General of our Institute, an office she held until her death, but she held it always against her will, and told me that she would very willingly have been a cook rather than carry that Cross of the Generalate. I also heard her say in public that she once wished to resign that office, but that the Pope had obliged her to remain in her post. I say with pleasure and satisfaction that she held the said office always in the most perfect manner.

p. 312

Many vocations flocked in from the beginning of her Institute. She required all information and all documents from the Postulants, not only as to their moral and spiritual state and that of their family, but also as to their physical state. I saw myself that she refused many. She talked much with the Postulants to know their disposition and character. Several Postulants did not do the Novitiate, among them I, but I heard the Servant of God say: «I have drawn more from those who did not make the Novitiate than from those who did. Believe me, now we keep them here in the Novitiate a whole year, but we have poorer vocations, whereas once, even without Novitiate, we had fine vocations».

§ 498
Visits to the houses of the Institute.

Four or five times I was present when the Servant of God made a visit to the houses, and I noticed that before anything else, even before greeting the Sisters, she went to the Church or Chapel to hear Holy Mass, if it was morning, or to receive the Blessing of the Blessed Sacrament, if it was evening. For this reason the Houses to which she was arriving were forewarned by telegram.

She diligently visited the whole House, also the wardrobe, the kitchen, the pantry, and listened to all the Sisters, and at the time of reading she gave a conference to the Sisters.

In the choice of offices the Servant of God had no respect of persons, but followed the aptitudes and capacities of each as she knew them. In the Chapters, however, she abided by the vote of the Sisters. So I saw myself.

I saw myself at Piacenza that the Servant of God took great care that her Sisters be well treated, and I saw her myself at Piacenza go into the kitchen, watch how the portions were made, and what there was for the Sisters. I heard her in the conferences to the Superiors say to us: «If you want very active and observant personnel, see to treating your sisters well in food and also in clothing». I remember, when we left, what outfits! Much clothing and all new. She wanted us to have nothing old.

In the first times of the Institute, however, there was a certain scarcity of food; the necessary, however, never failed us; and it is to be noted that I never heard the Sisters complain of the scarcity of those times; on the contrary, I heard of other houses, where I have not been, that they were then very content. The observance of the rule was more precise and exact then; and I heard the Servant of God exclaim: «Do you remember those times when we lacked so many things? How much more perfect the observance was than now, when we lack nothing».

§ 499
Development of the Institute and good administration.

Ad 23, Proc. fol. 1602v.: Our Institute spread most rapidly, notwithstanding all the difficulties and oppositions it had at the beginning from persons even of authority and from the Bishops themselves, as I have heard said, and I attribute this very rapid development to the prayers and merits of the Servant of God.

Mgr. Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, said to me one day: «I too once contradicted your Mother sometimes, but always for her good, and I always wished her so much good». As it happened to me to enter this Institute, which I did not know at first, so too I have heard it told by many Sisters that they also did not know the Institute before and that they found themselves led with great naturalness to enter this Institute: I do not remember the names, however.

The daughter Houses depended and depend on the Generalate House not only as to discipline but also as to administration, and if anything is left over it must be sent to the Generalate House. Every six months the cash account was given, and is given; if there was a surplus it was sent; if there was none, the Servant of God asked for nothing, at least as far as I know.

From personal experience I know that she praised only for the keeping of the accounts.

When I was at Spello, we were sometimes four, sometimes five Sisters. Our total monthly allowance was 60 lire. From this it is understood that we could send nothing to the Generalate House, but the Servant of God had to send us things to clothe ourselves. I know of no complaints by Sisters or Superiors made because the Mother asked for excessive economies in order to be able to send her more copious residues. When I was sent on visitation, as I narrated in another session, in listening to the Sisters, I never noticed any invitations or pressures, direct or indirect, from the Servant of God to have more copious residues.

The Servant of God did say, and recommended it, that superfluous expenses and superfluous gifts not be made, but if it were necessary to make them, they should be according to our state and conformable to our poverty.

p. 314

Ad 21, Proc. fol. 1604v.: The Servant of God possessed and exercised all the Theological and Cardinal virtues, and connected ones, Poverty, Chastity, Obedience and Humility.

§ 500
Most lively faith.

And beginning with Faith, I shall say that this was most lively in her, and she tried to enliven and kindle it, if the case arose, in others. She showed it by the solicitude with which she spoke to the Sisters, recommending catechism to children; by having sent her Sisters to Africa. In this connection I recall that once we were received, 180 Superiors, in Audience by the Holy Father Leo the Thirteenth in the year 1889. It was after the General Chapter. Present at that Audience was also Cardinal Alimonda, our Protector.

§ 501
Most loving of prayer, union with God.

The Pope, raising his hand toward the Servant of God, exclaimed: «Rosa, what have you done?», and the Servant of God: «What have I done? Nothing, Holy Father». And then the Pope, pointing to this band of Superiors, said: «You have prayed much, and this is the effect of prayer. Continue in prayer and in the observance of the Rule. We already have Houses in Africa. In those Missions do not be in a hurry to convert. Even if you converted one a year, it is already enough. Do not be in a hurry even to have the Unbelievers make the sign of the Holy Cross; let them come of themselves. Continue with prayer and with the observance of the rule, and the rest will come of itself».

She was most fond of prayer, and exhorted the others also to pray.

I noticed in her a particular recollection in prayer; I never saw her seated in the Chapel, but always kneeling on the floor, lightly with her hands resting on a chair. She was motionless in that position for the whole time of Mass.

Her union with God appeared not only in prayer but also in any other act of hers, and also in conversation. She recommended to her Sisters to say well the prayers of the Community. And she said this because she did not love novelties in devotions, nor that they be too numerous, and therefore when she visited the houses, if she found in the Chapels or Churches some novelty of devotion, she noted it with displeasure. «Be always united with God in prayer, — she told us. — I do not say that you should pray always, but it is union, continual union with God, that I want».

She recommended to us in a special way morning prayer from the very first rising from bed: «If the day is begun well with prayer, all will go well; if not, the day will go to pieces». She made meditation every day, and recommended to her daughters that they never omit it: «Neglect anything, but not daily meditation», she told us.

§ 502
Fame of holiness.

Ad 38, Proc. fol. 1633v.: While the Servant of God lived, she was esteemed by us Sisters a Saint, and we all had much veneration for her. For my part I can say that I held her for a Saint worthy of the Altars: I cannot say, however, whether, when the other Sisters called her a Saint, they had this same precise conception of mine. I also know that persons outside the Institute esteemed her much and held her in veneration. I was here when Bishops also came to be able to speak with her, and if they could not see her because she was absent or ill, they showed themselves grieved.

Sr. ANNA FARA MARTINENGO

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 1651, testis respondit:

§ 503
General particulars of the witness and scope of acquaintance.

My name is Anna Fara Martinengo, in the world Cesarina. I was born at Oreglia (Province of Porto Maurizio) on 11 March 1858, of the late Achille and Vittoria Grassi, good Christians.

When the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno was completing her twenty-fifth year of religious profession, I made my entrance into the Institute in this house of Via Merulana.

Already eight or ten years before, or five or six, coming to Rome I had made a courtesy visit (because I knew the family) to the young Marchioness Pomarici, who was here a Novice and is now Superior at our house of Cercola. I marveled at everything I saw and heard of the Sisters. I did go to Mass on Sundays and sometimes also during the week, provided however I had not spent the night in society, because then I sometimes arrived at the last Mass, and when it was no longer even valid. How my vocation then came to me I shall tell afterward, because it seems to me it is for the glorification of our Foundress.

Ad 7: I came to know the Servant of God when, once, finding myself in some friction with my mother, I thought of turning to her for counsel. And I therefore came to this house and was received by her in her study. The counsel I desired to have from the Servant of God was because my mother absolutely wanted me with her, and I, who through certain circumstances had been habitually away from home for six or seven years, could not resign myself to the diminution of the freedom I had enjoyed in those years, although even in that time I went into society either with the family of Count Nigra or with that of the Marquises Pomarici. I wanted to know from the Servant of God how I should behave with my mother, and I asked — or rather gladly accepted — the hospitality offered me, because it gave me a way to get away momentarily from my mother. I then chose Mother Gattorno as my counselor in this case because I had been told so much of her, in praise, both by the Novice Pomarici and by her uncle the Monsignor; and from him I then knew how much Mgr. Granito di Belmonte extolled her.

Proc. fol. 1657: In that first conversation I had with the Servant of God, as I said in the preceding session, I was struck by her bearing, above all by her eyes, which told me so many things; especially I was amazed because, while I, with pride and indifference, narrated to her all my adventures in the world, she was not at all shocked; on the contrary, she at once invited me to enter her Institute. I, who felt all the attractions of the world, objected that it would not be possible for me then to be a good Religious. She, however, assured me and encouraged me to enter with a certainty that surprised me. As, on leaving home that day, I had asked my mother's permission to be absent for a few days among the Daughters of St. Anne, with the pretext of a piece of work to do in homage to Mother Gattorno, whose twenty-fifth anniversary of Religious profession was approaching, that day therefore I stayed here, but without any intention of becoming a religious; on the contrary, that thought frightened me. I spoke often in the following days with the Servant of God, and seized any pretext to speak to her. She, without putting any pressure on me, invited me to try in the Novitiate.

Since when I was in the world I had taken the diploma of qualification for teaching natural sciences in the Higher Schools, besides the higher normal license, which I had already obtained at the age of fifteen. Therefore in religion I was assigned to teaching. Then I was destined for the administration of the Hospital of Peace in Naples, but before this the Servant of God had sent me to open an Institute at Macerata Feltria for technical schools, where I fell ill from excessive worry and the adverse climate, not wishing to call in outside Professors.

When I returned to this Generalate house in vacation time, the Servant of God had me act as her occasional Secretary, or rather as help for the Secretariat work, and in this office I learned to know her great soul, which revealed itself in her correspondence, in the dispatch of affairs.

p. 318

Proc. fol. 1663: After four years of teaching and three at the Hospital of Peace in Naples, and another three in Rome here in this house to teach a bit of everything to the Novices who were to leave for abroad and to the Sisters, I am now occupied with a small museum of natural sciences, and I also sometimes help an Assistant with her semi-official and family correspondence.

§ 504
Sufferings and poverty in the foundation.

Ad 17, Proc. fol. 1672: All said (and narrated particulars too) that the Servant of God had much to suffer in the first times of her foundation, materially, morally and spiritually.

The Servant of God had, for example, not even bed blankets to give to the sisters; and she deprived herself even of her own. The aforementioned Sr. Rosa told me that in those beginnings there was only one blanket, which naturally was reserved for the Servant of God, while the other four Sisters were without. The Servant of God deprived herself of hers and gave it to those four Sisters, who found themselves each with a blanket. Want was suffered in the kitchen, and the Sisters found themselves helped so many times unexpectedly by Providence, provisions arriving sometimes a short time before dinner. So the Sisters Rosa Dafrosa and the present portress of the mother house of Piacenza told me.

Many told me that the Servant of God had then to suffer morally too because not everyone attributed to her uprightness of intention. She was slandered. She suffered, moreover, above all when her Sisters were offended or insulted. «For myself, she said, it would be nothing».

Sr. Giorgia Bensi, who was one of the oldest, told me that in the beginnings at Piacenza they accused the Sisters of being bread-eaters, with no wish to work, gathered together to live off others.

§ 505
Humility.

Ad 22, Proc. fol. 1679: She was so vexed at hearing herself called Mother General, as she expressed it to me, and preferred the simple name of Mother. In order not to be vexed by the title of General, she did not think of it at all, and when they called her so, it was as if she did not hear that title. So she said to me.

I have heard many Sisters say that she tried to resign this office of Mother General, but did not succeed.

§ 506
A good superior, and prudent in the admission of postulants.

To the question how she fulfilled her office of Mother General, a poor Sister like me can only answer: in the most perfect and refined way.

The Servant of God was most cautious in the admission of Postulants; she took with great precision and exactness all the information, and I know it from personal experience. It is true, however, that sometimes the Servant of God was generous as regards the economic conditions of the Postulant.

When I was at the Hospital of Peace in Naples, I interested myself in a young lady of fifteen, daughter of a lawyer, of a very distinguished family, that she might be received into our Institute. On my recommendation the Servant of God accepted her. The young lady had the willing consent of her family; she prepared all her papers, all her things for departure; when behold a letter reaches me from the Servant of God, in which she says to me: «From well-placed persons I have learned, about the family of the young lady recommended by you, things that you never understood. Do me the charity of not putting such people in my house».

Sometimes I allowed myself to observe to the Servant of God that it would be fitting to pay a little attention to education in the admission of Postulants; but she rightly answered me: «It is true, my daughter, that we have many illiterate; but can we put you others to work in the kitchen or in other tiring services? Not for lack of virtue that there may be in you others, but through insufficiency of physical strength, one would groan here, another there, and these tiring but necessary services would not be done».

I heard some Sister make some small remark to the Servant of God about her prudence in the admission of Postulants; but unfortunately these Sisters who spoke so showed by leaving the Institute that a good spirit did not animate them.

I also saw, when I served the Servant of God as occasional Secretary, as I said in another session, how solicitous and prudent the Servant of God was in seeking precise information about the Postulants.

The great number of those who flocked to this our Institute must be attributed to its being a work of God, and not to the Servant of God's liberality in admissions, nor to the necessary moral qualities not being found in the Postulants.

p. 320

§ 507
She spared no labor in visiting the communities.

The Servant of God, as long as health permitted, visited her houses herself, and it can be said that she was always traveling. She did not spare herself in this even when ill, not even in the last year of her life; she traveled up to the whole of the October before her death. Not being able herself to go to some house, because they multiplied rapidly, she sent one of the Assistants or others in her place. I myself was present, in the evening, after her supper, when she invited this or that sister to send her as visitor to some house.

To the houses of America, and in general abroad (to France, however, she went herself), not being able to go herself, she delegated visitors with full powers, as I myself saw and heard from the Visitors themselves.

§ 508
Maternal spirit in the visits to the communities.

She then made her visits in the spirit of a mother and of a Superior. Once when I said to her: «Your visit to the houses is like that of a Bishop to his diocese, is it not?», she, with that good smile that distinguished her, answered me: «Oh! no, my daughter; my visits are those of a mamma to her little daughters. The Superiors of the houses can come to me and set everything before me; but it is not so easy for the other Sisters to come to me, therefore I go to them. I go to a central house, and have them come there. Sometimes I go to bring them the mamma's smile, and sometimes I go to carry away with me so many crosses».

Once, questioned by me about where she had been at a certain time, she told me that she had gone here and there, that she had worked much, that if I had seen her I would have exclaimed: «Poor Mother», that she had had days of battle, and that many people had been set in order.

During the visits she took measures, but the most energetic ones were taken by her afterward.

§ 509
Just in the distribution of offices.

Proc. fol. 1685: I believe it never occurred to any Sister either that the Servant of God distributed offices through partiality or fondness for someone. She distributed them with the greatest wisdom and as if enlightened. She always saw well what one was capable of and what one was not; and according to these views she governed herself.

§ 510
Prudent in founding new houses.

Ad 23: The Servant of God, when a new house was proposed to her, informed herself first of all in what way her daughters could fulfil their duties of piety. And she did not much concern herself with the economic provision made for the Sisters for the new house by those who invited them. I myself heard her repeat: «In the foundations of new houses it does not matter if we find ourselves in financial straits, we shall observe the rule and the vow of holy poverty better. Have confidence; work much for love of Jesus, pray much, and you will never lack anything».

She recommended that the Sisters in the new houses be very discreet; and that, being used to houses where nothing was lacking, they should not expect to find everything just so in the new houses: for example, a schoolteacher should not be alarmed because she lacked a bell. While, however, she recommended poverty so much, and did not mind accepting new houses with limited means, she nevertheless helped her daughters when they found themselves in real need. The Servant of God then always so much recommended poverty and kept watch on this point, not sparing the Superiors remarks when she saw that they had provided themselves with something that seemed to her luxury. I myself saw letters on this subject, and in them I saw, for example, remarks about a luxurious carpet. «A good sign, — she used to say —, when one is pinched in every way; when all goes well on every side, I do not like it so much».

§ 511
She watched that the sisters should not lack the necessary.

The Servant of God watched that the Sisters should not lack the necessary. How many times she sent cloth and other things, writing to the Superiors: «You will reimburse me when you can; now I know you are not in a position because you have other obligations». I know it because I myself saw it in the letters, and also because I heard her speak in this way.

Every house had to send the cash account to the Generalate House. If there was a cash surplus, the Servant of God either assigned it to the enlargement of that given house which had the surplus, or to better furnishing of the Church, or to improvement of the food for the boarding school of that house, or else it was given to the law of compensation between rich houses and poor, especially with our houses of health, which have no income at all and are opened exclusively for sick sisters.

§ 512
Moral and spiritual reports on the sisters.

The Servant of God required of the Superiors, I think once a year (so at least I saw and heard), a moral and spiritual report on their Sisters, even perpetually professed ones. It is needless to say that she required it much more for the Novices. And if a Superior had forgotten some perpetually professed in her report, the Servant of God wrote to her: «Why do you tell me nothing about such a Sister? Take care, for I want to be informed of everything, even the most insignificant things». She wanted to know also whether the professed were advancing in virtue or were stationary. Even to the stationary ones the Servant of God sent letters of reproof, and it fell to me to write several times, as it also fell to others, as for example to Sr. Anna Teresa Sorrentino.

When, however, she entrusted me or others with these letters (in which sometimes she recommended energetic and strong language and said to me, for example: «Write to her in good strong ink, do not spare her»), she committed the address to another, and she herself then closed the letter in the envelope, and so the one who wrote the letter did not come to know to whom the reproofs were addressed. To me she made the address known only once, the first time perhaps, because I was moved by the harshness of the reproof I had been commissioned to write. She then recommended that I never disclose the name to others, although I did not know her. I must also say that in that letter it was not a matter of grave things, but of small infractions of religious discipline.

Sr. Anna Teresa Sorrentino then told me that she had never known any address of those letters of reproof which she had written by commission of the Servant of God.

Besides the annual moral and spiritual report, of which I have spoken, the Servant of God wanted to be informed of any novelty. She invited in a particular way the Sisters residing far away abroad to confidence toward her, to write to her without hesitation, without circumlocutions; and she wrote and said to them: «Have you no pains to confide to me? Let us thank Jesus; have you no joys? Share them with me, we shall thank Jesus together, and always write to me».

I saw sometimes, when the cash surpluses of the houses of one of our communities reached the Servant of God, and I never noticed that she took pleasure in it, since it was simply a duty fulfilled by the Superiors. Once, however, when a Superior had sent a fair surplus, the Servant of God wrote to her: «You have made yourself look fine by sending me the rest of the cash, while I have learned that the Sisters have no shawl for the winter. You send them all stained, it is a pity. Oh, shame! One sees you have neither head nor heart!». This letter I wrote myself. To give a fuller idea of the maternal solicitude the Servant of God had for her Sisters, I shall speak also of another letter that she had me write for a Superior: «I know from a well-placed person that the nursing Sisters who spent the night away from home find even the coffee cold in the morning. And is it the same for you? No, I imagine. See, I also know other things more serious than these, I shall tell you another time. Put yourself in the presence of God: divine justice is one for all».

§ 513
Solicitude for the sick sisters. Complaints of some.

When the Sisters were sick, and she knew that the Superiors were in real financial straits, she wrote: «I know that you truly cannot buy the medicines, which the administration does not cover, because they are specialty drugs and cost an arm and a leg; I know that the Sister and you yourself need more substantial nourishment; do not skimp, buy what is needed, for God will provide. Do not be afraid that the ground will give way under your feet. You must be well, because there will still be a great deal of work to do». More than once I myself wrote in this sense by commission of the Servant of God, and I also heard more than once when she gave a similar commission to others.

When some Sister complained about food or clothing, and the complaints reached the Servant of God, she supported her, if she deserved it, and remedied; if she was not worthy of a hearing, she admonished and reproved her, as I heard from the one who wrote, by commission of the Servant of God: «I hear that you always complain, you are never content, I have changed your house oh how many times in a few months: pantry and kitchen always have the door wide open for you alone, and you, indiscreet, have the courage to complain? What a pity! I no longer know what to do! I shall pray God to send you his sweetnesses. What kind of Sister are you? You make me pity you!».

I can say with full knowledge and conscience that there were very few Sisters who complained of scanty treatment. And this I know because, finding myself several times with the Servant of God here and there in the houses, I came to know in confidence how the Sisters fared; and also I knew it from the passage of Sisters through this Generalate House, where from time to time I was.
