§ 514
Maternal spirit toward her children in the flesh.

Ad 24, Proc. fol. 1692v.: The Servant of God loved her children in the flesh with the most tender affection, according to the law of God, understood in the highest sense of the expression, offering to him the joys and the tortures of her heart as a woman and an earthly mother in order to create for herself a marvelous spiritual offspring, solely to magnify the glory of God with admirable works of charity. I knew almost the whole family that remained to her from the twenty-fifth year of the foundation of the Institute.

The brothers Francesco and Federico loved their sister very much, esteemed her greatly and revered her; Francesco almost with the bearing of a son rather than of a brother. Over Federico the Servant of God had great ascendancy.

I found myself sometimes at family gatherings in which the two brothers, the Barbiellinis and some Sister took part. The Servant of God, however, did not welcome these large gatherings, as she once told me, and I shall never forget it.

This love toward relatives was not at the expense of what she owed to her Sisters, and I heard her daughter Carlotta say, all excited and in tears: «Mamma love much her Sisters: I jealous; Mamma give too much to the nuns, I greedy, I want (this or that) and Mamma give nothing to me; give little, Carlotta unhappy!».

On occasions of happy circumstances she did not favor her relatives, and did not even attend baptisms! So Sr. Anna Maria Teresa Sorrentino told me.

On occasions of illness or mourning she visited her relatives accompanied by her Sisters; and whoever saw her attested to me that the Servant of God, in serving her sick, who were blood of her blood (as in the last illness and death of her son Alessandro and of a little nephew of hers), brought help, the word of God, and comfort with that heroic virtue with which she lavished them on all the sick in general. With extraordinary self-mastery, she held in check the sensibility of her extremely affectionate heart.

Her son Alessandro had led a worldly life, and the Servant of God had labored much to draw him from it; in the end, however, she obtained that he should die as a good Christian. I have heard it said that the Servant of God had her brother Federico regularize his marriage.

p. 325

The Servant of God, as I have heard from several Sisters of the house of Piacenza, gave her daughter Carlotta all that she herself had had as dowry, which cannot have been negligible, if one thinks that the boarding school where she put her daughter in education charged a quite considerable fee. And I know nothing more.

§ 515
She made no conspicuous gifts to relatives.

I do not know that the Servant of God made conspicuous gifts to her relatives, or even to her daughter, on some extraordinary occasion, but only those gifts that are customary in good families.

Small gifts the Sisters still made to the Barbiellini family, but these, at least with me, were returned in gentlemanly fashion. Those of the Barbiellini family often came to the house, all the more as their dwelling was adjacent to ours, both here and at Piacenza. The Servant of God, however, never received them at working time, and even after having let them in, because she found herself free, she dismissed them at once, or withdrew herself, if another person arrived who had to speak with her, or telegrams, etc.

She did not want her little nephews to make noise in our house.

Many evenings some of her family came, among others the nephew Dino with a companion of his, and Professor Ferrario. The first time I was present, Dino's companion allowed himself to begin an attack on our Religion, and cited Voltaire. The Servant of God at this name grew dark in the face and rose up with youthful ardor to rebut that impertinent fellow, and her speaking turned into a splendid lecture on the faith. I was present several times at similar conversations. The speaking of the Servant of God was always most instructive, on one subject or another.

Ad 27, Proc. fol. 1700: As to the virtues, I should like to use an inexact expression, but one that expresses my thought; namely that the Servant of God personified all the virtues, that is, Faith, Hope, Charity, Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, Temperance, Chastity, Poverty, Obedience and Humility, and others.

§ 516
A burning torch of living faith.

And beginning with Faith, the Servant of God was a burning torch, continual, living, most living. She had only one ideal: God and his glory. I myself heard her, speaking in a particular way to the Sisters who were leaving for the missions, exhort them with burning words to be ready to give even life and blood for the faith. Once she was ill. She came to the Novitiate, while I too was there, and when she spoke of the faith it seemed that every symptom of illness had vanished from her; indeed she seemed rejuvenated.

She seemed the perpetual companion of the Nazarene in teaching catechism. I myself heard her, even in the parlor, neglect no occasion to teach and instruct about our faith.

The Servant of God had wished that a congregation of the Daughters of Mary be established at this very Generalate House of ours, and I myself saw with how much love she occupied herself with their religious instruction. She spent recreation with them, entertaining them with pleasant and edifying conversation, and these recreations she had the Daughters of Mary hold in order to attract them more easily. She took care to have suitable preachers for them. I heard her when she said to us: «Have you little girls of various ages? Your speaking with them must always be full of faith, ardent and simple, and strong, but always proportioned to the various ages of your little girls». I also know that before being a Religious, the Servant of God occupied herself much with the Daughters of Mary, as I said in another session, and with true missionary zeal already from then.

§ 517
She desired the conversion of all to the true faith.

I heard her several times express her ardent desire that all should be converted to the true faith. For this she sent her Sisters as Missionaries to Africa. The recommendations she made to her departing Sisters were superlatively beautiful, that they should never spare themselves, at the cost of giving their lives. She often repeated to us: «Oh, how beautiful it is to die for the faith! This is the most glorious death a Sister can have!».

Faith she called the most precious gift we have from God; and once I remember that she told me that the greatest charity we can do is that faith be not lost: «Oh, the torture, she told me, that one feels when one sees a dying person who has little more time to return to the Lord and still does not profit by it. Were it not for the grace of God, I could not bear it, and should die of grief!».

It was faith that drove her when she accepted houses whose financial means were scanty, if the field of work was wide. So that the Daughters of Mary might find good pasture and not be tempted to read perverse books, she began a circulating library in this generalate house.

§ 518
Teaching and practice of the Servant of God on prayer.

Proc. fol. 1707v.: Concerning prayer, she used all the most effective comparisons to move her Sisters to insist upon it, to fall in love with it, and so to be able in the hidden life to taste the beauties of the faith. «Prayer is the door of paradise, — she used to repeat; — prayer is the key that opens the door of the Heart of Jesus; prayer is also the voice that lets you feel whether you have observed the Holy Rule». So one day I said to her: «So, Mother, prayer is the panacea for all ills». «Oh, — the Servant of God resumed, — you may well say it, prayer is the remedy for all ills, but it is also the reward of that which you would wish to accomplish with greater perfection».

In the conferences that the Servant of God came to give to the Novitiate and to the Superiors during the General Chapter, I remember they turned almost always on the observance of some point of the rule, supported by prayer: «Take heed, daughters, she said, in joy, in sorrow, in trials, in work, always lean on prayer. And I urge you, do not bring so many tears to Jesus (unless these are tears of repentance). Be on your guard, daughters, in joys. When one is very happy, one does not pray with the same spirit, with the same fervor as when one is in distress».

When the Servant of God prayed, she was like a statue. I observed her with great wonder, in the first years especially at Piacenza, and to me it was incredible. How many times in our Chapel at Piacenza I observed minutely the posture of the Mother in prayer, and even how many bricks she covered with her habit (note that she always knelt on the floor); then I would leave the chapel, go to have breakfast, then go for a walk, and two hours later I returned to the Chapel to check the position of the Servant of God, and I always found her in that same, exactly the same position as before.

§ 519
Devotions of the Servant of God, expressions of her faith.

Proc. fol. 1731v.: And now, to speak of the devotion of the Servant of God to the Second Person of the Most Holy Trinity, I shall say that she was so devoted to the divine Child, spoke of him with such fervor, that one could not but fall in love with him. She presided over and directed the setting up of the crib in our Church, which was done with much art; and at that time it seemed that this thought occupied her all day, and she made use of everything to speak of the Child Jesus. She invited us all, at that time, to stay with the shepherds (her talks always came back to this), to love the hidden life and to despise the world. The glory of the shepherds, she told me, surpasses that of the Magi and of all the great of the earth, and this because I had expressed to her my preference for a life with the Magi. Before the Child Jesus is the pasture of the whole interior life: there is Mary and there is Joseph. And here she brought out the holiness and greatness of Mary and Joseph, spoke of their devotion, and then her talk went on to the Eternal Father, who made the humility of St. Joseph and of Our Lady shine forth, and she added many other things. She spoke of the devotion of St. Francis to the Child Jesus. For the feast of Holy Christmas she gave great importance to favoring the friends of the Institute. On the night of Holy Christmas she seemed to grow young again, and to draw fresh vigor from the holy conversations she held with us. On these occasions it seemed that charity grew in her, and she gave, gave to all, as long as she could.

§ 520
Devotion to St. Anne.

I was present, on the day before Christmas Eve, at the extraordinary distribution of articles to the poor, in which the Mother was helped by other Sisters; and the joy of giving largely to her dear poor shone so on her face as to give it an aspect of new beauty. «Give, give freely, — she said —, in the holy name of the Child Jesus, for He will be generous with us like a Sovereign».

Proc. fol. 1747v.: Joined to that to Our Lady was the dutiful devotion that she paid to St. Anne, our Mother, and she wanted her Sisters too to pay it.

Her cult of St. Anne was so ardent and communicative that we felt stimulated to imitate her. This devotion of hers is attested by the letters in which she recommended it to us; in the month of St. Anne, moreover, she forgot years and troubles to be wholly with her daughters in honoring the Holy Mother. Surprising, moreover, was the activity of her mind to be informed of every particular that had been done in our Houses in honor of the Holy Mother for her feast.

I was present sometimes two or three days after the said feast, when the Servant of God had not yet received from some house the report of what the Sisters had done on that feast. She gave herself no peace until she had all the reports, and wrote, taking any pretext, perhaps to give an insignificant order, in order to let the Superiors know that she was still awaiting the desired report.

On the eve of the feast, one year, seeing her all busy, I followed her everywhere, as I could, to catch some thought of hers and to be edified; and at a certain moment I asked her what she thought would be the most beautiful part of the feast the next day; but she in turn asked me: and I told her various things, and finally the Mass. Then she dwelt on this thought, waiting for me to add something else, then she added: «the Mass of the vows». And here she spoke to me with an unforgettable accent, dwelling on the mystery of the union of the soul with Jesus by means of the Holy Vows. Especially in the month of St. Anne the ardor with which she spoke of her is incredible. If she was at the desk and intent on writing, she would lay down the pen and draw back, making the chair creak, so that it gave me the impression that she wished to yield her place to the Holy Mother. We felt the duty of gratitude and thanked her for any favor she granted us; and she, although she welcomed our thanks, then yielded the place to St. Anne, saying: «I deserve nothing; it was the Holy Mother who wished it so, who counseled it so». And once I heard her say: «I am not even the instrument to work that little good that is done in our Institute; it is the Holy Mother who works everything. Let us go about holily humble at being her daughters».

§ 521
Veneration for the Pope and the ecclesiastical authorities.

Proc. fol. 1757: For Authority, and in the first place for the Pope, her respect was profound, moving. And she did not fail not only to exhort the Sisters, but also lay people, when they came, to ask for an audience of the Holy Father, public or private, so that they might have occasion to see him close up, and thus dispel from their minds all the evil gossip against the Pope. «Let us bring, — she said —, as many people as we can to see the Pope».

I heard from Sr. Anna Antonietta Gallinari, deceased, formerly Superior of our House in the Parish of the Fornaci, tell with what rapture the Servant of God spoke of Pio Nono, and that she regarded him as the Founder of the Institute.

p. 330

I saw the Servant of God show herself radiant with happiness because, to her question as to who the Pope was, a little dark-skinned girl of seven had answered: «He is the Vicar of Jesus Christ».

That time when, after the General Chapter, she led her hundred and eighty Superiors to Pope Leo the Thirteenth, it seemed that she with her Institute offered him her heart, her unconditional devotion.

On the tomb of Pio Nono there is in mosaic also the coat of arms of our Institute, which reveals to us not only the offering given by the Servant of God for that sepulchre, but also her devotion and gratitude to Pio Nono.

She paid her devotion and obedience not only to the Holy Father but also to his representatives, that is, to his College of Cardinals, and first of all to the Cardinal Protector. She made known to the Sisters the fine qualities and characteristics and the merits of the Cardinal Protectors toward the Institute, even of those whom we had not had the good fortune to know personally. I remember the recommendations she made to the Sisters, that they should revere with great honor their Cardinal, if they had the good fortune to have him as Pastor of the Diocese in which they were, and to these Cardinals resident in the Diocese she took care to bring the homage not only of those few Sisters who were in that Diocese, but also of the whole Institute. I have seen several letters on this. And she was so delicate toward them that once, as I recall, she noticed that there was not much space between the date and the signature of a letter to a Cardinal, and remarked that in that lack of etiquette there was a lack of regard for the high dignity of the Cardinal.

§ 522
Hope and perfect resignation to the divine will.

Proc. fol. 1765: Hope and trust were virtues deeply penetrating her, which made the crosses vanish for her. She was always therefore in the most perfect and complete resignation to the will of God in every event, and she told us that, in order always to have complete resignation, we must always hold the will of God as our own. In the grave difficulties of the Institute, such as the closing of houses, or negotiations that were not going well for the opening of others, I never saw her cast down in spirit; on the contrary, I sometimes heard her say: «You distress yourselves so much, and I am glad, because from the very difficulties I see that Jesus protects us».

When she received letters announcing illnesses of Sisters, or exhaustion of physical strength, she said to reply to them that she left them prayer and hope as medicine.

Many times the Servant of God found herself pressed by large payments or by other financial needs, but hope in Jesus comforted her so much that she said to us: «Oh, let us really not think about that! Jesus will not fail to help us».

We then verified that this her unlimited trust in the Lord was crowned by extraordinary successes.

§ 523
She instilled confidence in the hearts of others.

She knew how to instill so much confidence in the Lord in the hearts of others that, as I heard from many mothers of families, after speaking with her they went away all consoled, full of confidence that they would not be abandoned by the Lord.

Mgr. Pomarici told of various persons who had received extraordinary help merely for having entrusted themselves to the Servant of God.

I have already spoken of her great union with God, which already shows her charity.

§ 524
Ardent love of God.

I never saw in her any imperfection. And she recommended to Sisters and lay people not only to keep watch so as to remain free from any fault, but also exhorted them to abstain from some things, even lawful ones, in order to earn merits and to acquire a higher degree of love of God.

She exhorted us to the disinterested love of Jesus. «We must not, — she said to us —, give to him in order to receive, but give and offer disinterestedly and out of pure love and gratitude».

She was moved, even struck dumb, when she heard blasphemies or other things offensive to God. «At these offenses, — she said —, if the Eternal Father were capable of weeping, he would weep tears of blood, as my soul weeps». She exhorted us to procure reparation for them, either by having a child or a gravely ill person pray, or by seeking to profit from a good moment to lift a strayed soul to God with some good word.

According to the qualities of the persons she gave exhortations that they should return to God, while God would then assist them in the needs in which they found themselves.

Her charity toward her neighbor was the proverbial well of St. Patrick, inexhaustible.

§ 525
Various manifestations of charity toward her neighbor.

Proc. fol. 1770v.: The charity of the Servant of God turned to all social classes.

At Naples especially, many little girls left destitute found asylum through the insistent recommendations of the Servant of God.

I have heard of two cases of pious young women who, not being able to be admitted into our Institute, I do not know for what reasons, and wishing on the other hand to become nuns, were helped by the Servant of God to be admitted elsewhere in Religious Houses.

Her charity also showed itself in the disaster of Casamicciola, by sheltering many little girls, as the Vice-Superior of our house at Naples, Sr. Anna Ianuaria, still living at Villa St. Anne, told me.

Also to youths who showed an inclination to the ecclesiastical state and who could not go on for lack of means, the Servant of God gave help, as I recall in particular of one from Conversano, Mr. Giuseppe Falchi, who still calls himself the first beneficiary of Mother Gattorno.

The first Sisters narrated the touching way in which the Servant of God dispensed charity during the cholera at Piacenza. She went personally, early in the morning, with her first Secretary, entering laden with linen the families of the needy sick.

In one winter, at Piacenza, she personally distributed soup to hundreds of poor. So said the elderly Sr. A. Rosa, Sr. A. Dafrosa, Sr. A. Giorgia Bensi, Sr. A. Leonzia and many others. I have heard lay people say: «Mother Gattorno gives and gives always, without having, and then always has inexhaustibly».

In many cases I heard by word of mouth, and saw also in letters, that the Servant of God came to the aid not only of our Sisters attached to the Hospital, but also of the patients of the Hospitals themselves, who could no longer, for the moment, be maintained by those administrations. So Sr. A. Leonzia, besides various small hospitals, speaking of that of Peace in Naples, said: «We Sisters, when the Hospital was in debt up to its eyes, never lacked anything, thanks to the charity of our Mother».

In the extraordinary visits that the Servant of God made to the sick, besides the objects of devotion that she distributed, she had more abundant food given.

§ 526
Evangelical prudence.

Proc. fol. 1787: The Servant of God possessed prudence not in the human sense but in the evangelical. In granting or denying permissions this virtue showed itself. To Sr. Anna Maria Stella Calderoni, who on a given occasion asked her permission for certain penances, she refused it, because of the delicacy of her physique. So I heard and also read in some letter. Whereas to another Sister, who asked her a similar permission, she not only granted it but even urged her to extraordinary penances. Her prudence was admirable in keeping peace in our Houses, and through this virtue many cases that seemed desperate were settled well. So once she set right by her prudence a Magistrate who had harassed our Sisters so much, as I myself heard from the Servant of God: «With one glance at the Tabernacle, she told me then, I set everyone right». Her prudence shone in having legally arranged the possessions of the Institute in such a way that it could not be despoiled by the intrigues of others. So one can see from the Process brought by the Barbiellini family.

Though she was so frank that she made known to us Sisters all the affairs of the Institute, she nevertheless kept silent, with great prudence, about things that could have hindered her government if they were known. So once, in the presence of a certain Superior, she did not wish to say where a Sister was, while the others present mistook in indicating the house.

If from strict duty she had to take some measure of severity, she took good care not to offend either social proprieties or the honor of the Sisters. So when she had to remove some Sister from a house, a measure to which outsiders, even powerful ones, were opposed, she held to reasons that could offend no one. She was admirable in the devices she used when relatives of Sisters tiresomely asked her that their Sister relatives be sent to this or that house nearer to them, or employed in this or that office. She, with patience, with skill, in replying, found the way to convince them of the inopportuneness of their requests.

Her prudence shines in having known how to hide for forty years the sufferings and the mortifications of her body.

Once, for the Corpus Christi Procession, which fell on a day of strike in Rome, she had the Procession file out, going herself in front, the first, from our gate to the door of the Church. We were all surprised and amazed, and all of us said: «The heart of our Mother was dominated by the thought of God, and not by human prudence». And it must be noted that all went well.

I saw many letters of hers to the Cardinal of Ferrara, in which she asked counsel; and not only did she defer to the opinion of such personages, but also to that of her Sister Assistants, as I myself learned from them. Not only did she keep to this system, but writing to the Superiors she impressed upon them not to act on their own, and if her maternal counsel was not enough, to turn either to the diocesan Bishop or to the Cardinal Protector, according to the nature of the affairs. «I myself, — she wrote to them —, have my companions in work, and to these I turn for counsel, although you say that I can do everything by myself». I noted, in the correspondence of the Cardinal of Ferrara, that although the Servant of God deferred to his opinion in disagreements, and had already begun the proceedings according to the Cardinal's counsel, in practice her own opinion always ended by prevailing, as the better one, if I remember rightly.

She had a special cult to Our Lady of Good Counsel, and in the Novitiate she always assigned this name to some sister.

The letters I have seen attest how her counsel was sought by ladies even in affairs that had nothing to do with religious matters; and one sees in them her expert eye, and her soul always turned to God and to leading to good.

§ 527
She practiced justice perfectly.

The Servant of God possessed the virtue of justice in the most perfect way, not only toward God but also toward men. She never denied the workers their due wage, and said rather to her Sisters: «If you are short of means, limit yourselves in alms, but as to the workers be generous», and I myself heard her. She distributed offices without regard to human respect; she gave corrections with just measure and timeliness. Her gratitude and thankfulness made her pour out thanks to Superiors and benefactors. Her phrase was this: «I do not know how to say anything, I cannot thank enough, but the Lord will surely see to rewarding her». She also insisted much that the Superiors should exercise justice scrupulously so as to give no handle even to the ill-disposed, whether in the hospitals or in the boarding schools, and reminded them of gratitude as a duty. She never tired of thanking the administrators of some hospital, if they had thought they should not charge her the expenses of some Sister sent by her for some operation, and had wished to keep her and treat her as a guest. And her thanks did not cease even for things of much less account. She enjoined the Sisters that prayers be said for the benefactors; and if someone failed to recite after dinner the three Glory Be's for the benefactors, she pointed out not only the failure to the rule but also that to gratitude.

§ 528
Strong in adversities.

The Servant of God was strong both in joys and in adversities. We Sisters always saw her upright and never bowed under the weight of difficulties and of the gravest sorrows, although her heart was most sensitive. We noticed it especially in the period of the Apostolic Visitation, when some weaker Sister lived in anxieties and palpitations; and she, with her calm, was our strength.

Sometimes sorrows wrung tears from her, but they did not succeed in taking from her resignation to the divine will. So those who saw her at the bedside of her dead son Alessandro told me. So I saw her, when the telegrams reached her announcing the death of the Superior Sr. Anna of Comfort (in America), the death of Sr. Anna Dafrosa, and others. And when these sorrowful tidings reached her, in which she saw grave losses for the Institute and her maternal heart grieved, she spoke to us of the duty of conforming ourselves to the divine will. It seemed incredible how a human creature could have so much mastery over herself.
